With barely enough time to rehearse, they managed to prepare a few Margis to act in the drama.

Despite the hasty preparation, the team did a credible job of staging the drama before an audience of about five hundred Margis, who roared with laughter at the rib-tickling scenes of social satire. The drama was rendered even more entertaining by the hilarious blunders of the ill-prepared actors. The Margis thoroughly enjoyed it especially because it poked fun at the

twin social problems of the social injunction against widow remarriage and the abominable dowry system. It was the first time a social event had been staged at the Marga's spiritual gatherings. Eventually, such programs to create social awareness became a regular feature of the Marga's spiritual functions like the DMC. Baba also enjoyed the drama from the window of his room on the second floor of Narasingh's house.

Shortly after the drama ended, it was announced that Baba would soon be addressing the gathering. The announcement was followed by a resounding chorus of '*Parama Pita Baba Ki, Jai*' from the expectant crowd waiting for him to arrive. Manas was sitting in the front row with some senior Margis, who on Pranay's instruction were keeping an eye on him. As Baba stepped into the hall, Manas craned his neck, eager to have a glimpse of the guru. When he saw only his dada walking towards the stage accompanied by Pranay and Narasingh, he asked the Margi seated next to him, "Where is the gurudev, Baba Anandamurti?"

"Don't you see the person in *dhoti* and *kurta* accompanied by the general secretary, Pranayda? He is the gurudev Baba." When he heard that his dada was indeed the mysterious guru of Ananda Marga, Manas became highly emotional and let out a piercing shriek. Overwhelmed by the discovery, he fell into a state of ecstasy. Not knowing what had happened to Manas, Sukumar Bose, who had been keeping a close watch on him, reported his abnormal condition to Baba. Baba replied that there was nothing to worry about and assured him that Manas would recover in due course. He instructed that Manas should be left alone.

After a few devotional songs Baba started his discourse, "Parama Purusha, the Supreme Consciousness, is my Father; Parama Prakrti, the Supreme Operative Principle, is my Mother and the universe is my homeland. We are all citizens of this universe."

Baba supported his assertion by explaining the relationship of every human being with the rest of creation and with the Creator.

"The universe is the thought projection of the Macrocosmic Mind. When an individual imagines an object, then that person alone and no one else is the owner of the object. As the universe is the thought projection of the Supreme Entity (Macrocosmic Nucleus), the ownership of the universe lies with the Supreme Entity, and not with His imagined beings. None of the movable or immovable properties of this universe belongs to any particular individual; everything is the common patrimony of all, and the Father of all is the Supreme Entity. All living beings can enjoy their rightful share of this property, like members of a joint family[^1].

"We must not forget, even for a single moment, that the entire animate world is a vast joint family. Nature has not assigned any portion of this property to any particular individual. Private ownership has been created by selfish opportunists, as the loopholes in this system provide them with ample scope for self-aggrandisement through exploitation. When the entire wealth of the universe is the common patrimony of all living beings, can a system in which some roll in luxury while others who are deprived of even a morsel of food shrivel up and starve to death bit by bit, be said to have the support of Dharma? In a joint family, every member is provided with adequate food, clothing, education and medical treatment as well as other amenities depending on their individual needs and the financial capacity of their family. If, however, any member of the family appropriates more grains, clothes, books or medicines than he requires, will that person not be the cause of distress to the other members of the family? In such circumstances, such actions will certainly be against Dharma; that will certainly be antisocial.

"A member of a joint family cannot be called a social being if he does not have a sentiment of oneness with the other members or does not want to embrace the lofty ideal of

[^1]: A joint family is a group of people living under one roof who eat food cooked in one pot, who hold property in common, and who are related to each other in one way or another.

joint rights and the principle of rationality. According to true spiritual ideology, the system of private ownership cannot be accepted as absolute and final, and hence capitalism cannot be supported.

"The ambition to become rich by exploiting others is a type of psychic disease. In fact, if the infinite longing of the human mind does not find a path that leads to psychic and spiritual fulfilment, it becomes engaged in accumulating excessive physical wealth by depriving others. If any member of a joint family appropriates food from the larder through physical or intellectual force, he becomes the cause of misery to the other members of the family. Similarly, when capitalists declare, 'We have amassed wealth by our talent and labor. If others have the capacity and diligence, let them also do the same; nobody is stopping them,' they do not care to realize that the volume of commodities on the earth is limited, whereas minimum requirements are common to all. Excessive individual affluence, in most cases, deprives others of the minimum requirements of life.

"As members of a joint family, human beings should safeguard this collective property in a befitting manner and utilize it properly. They should also arrange for everyone to enjoy it equally and ensure that all beings have the minimum requirements of life to enable them to live in a healthy body with a sound mind. We cannot neglect even a single living being in this creation, nor can we ignore the smallest part of the universe."

Baba then entered into a discussion on the need for economic democracy and decentralization as it was central to the new socio-economic vision he was gradually developing. In his view, the concept of economic democracy required a fundamental shift in thinking that would place the planning, implementation, management and decision-making processes in the hands of local people. The central idea behind economic democracy was a shift in the ownership of the economy from powerful conglomerates and governments to local people, and the need for production to be based on consumption and not on profit. The needs of the local people should be the main focus of production. Such an idea was completely new in India at that time, as the dominant ideologies were capitalism and communism, both of which promoted economic centralisation. Baba's vision of the economy emphasized among other things that the industrial system should be organized in accordance with the principle of decentralization.

He also proposed industrial and agricultural self-reliance through a restructuring of the economy into self-sufficient economic zones based on shared cultural and economic features. Planning for development should be done at the block-level and not at the national level. Each economic zone would have a network of efficient cooperatives. At that time in India a number of experimental cooperatives were running, but the initiative failed because they were either overly dependent on the whims of corrupt managers or were beset with difficulties created by the government and powerful industrialists. Baba advocated the creation of a network of cooperatives through which a major section of the economy would function. Complex or key industries, such as mining, would be managed by the local government and only small enterprises would be in the hands of private owners. All the other industries should be managed through cooperatives.

The Margis gathered in that small village of Trimohan were very surprised to hear Baba speak on a subject other than spirituality. While those who had had the opportunity for closer interaction with him were aware of his revolutionary ideas on a wide range of social issues, this was the first time they heard him speak specifically on social or economic issues. No one in that gathering could even remotely imagine that the revolutionary ideas he expressed that day were the precursor to an all-encompassing socio-economic and political philosophy based on a universal outlook that he would later expound. Indeed, in the very first line of his discourse in Trimohan, he had introduced the essence of his economic theory. That line became the cornerstone of the social philosophy he propounded more than a year later.

The next day during his morning walk, Baba further clarified what he had said the previous night. As he walked along the banks of the river Ganges with some local Margis, he suddenly stopped and turned to the Margis who were struggling to keep up with him. He asked, "Did you follow my discourse last night?"

"Yes Baba, a little," one of them replied.

"You see, what can a human being do? Human beings cannot create anything original. They cannot create the five fundamental factors that the universe is composed of. All they are capable of doing is to make physical mixtures and chemical compounds from what has already been created by Parama Purusha, the Supreme Father. He created the entire universe, all the innumerable galaxies, stars and planets. He created this planet and made it suitable for humans to live on thousands of millions of years before their arrival. Now if a few individuals, who have come on this planet for only a short period, try to assert, 'We are the owners of this physical world,' is there anything more foolish than that? It is nothing but the height of ignorance and arrogance. They are blinded by self-interest."

Slightly raising his voice, Baba stated emphatically, "Sooner or later, everyone will have to accept that not only this planet but also the entire universe is the collective patrimony of all living beings and not of the human race alone. It is absolutely essential to build a society based on this concept if living beings are to survive on this earth." To the Margis walking with him who were struggling to imbibe his new ideas, it sounded like a prophetic declaration.

During the morning gathering of the 26th, Baba announced the formation of a new organization he called Renaissance Universal (RU). It was the first subsidiary wing of Ananda Marga to be established, and its main objective was to provide a platform for intellectuals to discuss the diverse issues facing society, suggest solutions and create a new awakening in society.

After his discourse Baba convened a special meeting of the educated Margis, youths and students. He told them that in order to revitalise society, it was imperative to bring about an intellectual awakening amongst the educated people, the youth and the students, and to urge them to take on the responsibility of promoting progressive thinking amongst the general populace. He said that the main duty of the Renaissance Universal movement was to liberate educated people, the youth and the students from the shackles of the various dogmas that plagued society and to inculcate in them the ability to think logically and rationally.

He declared that the higher social and human values had been corroded by dogmas, and that their absence had created selfishness, narrowness and hatred between people. Blinded by dogma, they were destroying each other, other living beings and the environment, and ultimately becoming the cause of their own annihilation. Hence the struggle against all kinds of dogma was a prerequisite for building a new society based on moral and spiritual values. He urged the Margis to establish RU Clubs in their respective areas and to organize discussions on issues affecting the life of the general public.

In a discourse entitled "Renaissance in All the Strata of Life" which he gave on the 2nd of January 1986, Baba summarized the aims of RU as follows:

"The real meaning of the word 'renaissance' is reawakening. Humanity has been sleeping, and now it must wake up from its Cimmerian slumber and become active in all spheres of life, in all the strata of existence - the physical, the psychic and the spiritual.

"Nowadays science generally refers to the creation of new weapons which strengthen the hands of warmongers. The real spirit of social progress is to dispel all social disparities. Each and every member of society should enjoy equal rights as members of the same family, but at present there is a glaring disparity, and it is the duty of the Renaissance movement to dispel that disparity and bring about equality amongst human beings. Society should have cooperative leadership, not subordinated leadership. The Renaissance people will have to immediately start a movement to fight against all these disparities; for example, if fifty percent of the population who are women remain downtrodden, how can there be all-round

social progress? So these are the social duties, the social responsibilities of the Renaissance movement. The Renaissance people will have to wage war against these disparities, these inequalities; they will have to be rooted out of society."

The events during the Trimohan DMC and following it were indeed a revelation of sorts to the Margis. It slowly dawned on some of the more educated Margis present at the DMC that Baba intended Ananda Marga to be far more than just another conventional organization propagating spiritual philosophy, social reform and meditation. They realized that through his teachings, he was creating a blueprint to restructure all aspects of society.

One day during his Field Walk in Jamalpur shortly after the Trimohan DMC Baba spoke about the defects of communism and capitalism. "Capitalism is a defective philosophy just like communism. Both have been the cause of great human suffering. Another consequence of these materialistic philosophies is the grave degeneration of values. A time will come when people will reject both these defective philosophies."

The Margis found it difficult to relate to what Baba had just said about the fate of capitalism and communism because all the political, economic and social systems of the day were based on one or the other of these ideologies. Pranay was the first to voice his opinion, "Baba, both communism and capitalism are extremely powerful forces."

"Pranay, no force on earth, no matter how powerful, can prevent the demise of communism and capitalism. As it is the inexorable decree of Parama Purusha, it is sure to happen."

"Will they both disappear at the same time?" inquired Pranay.

"No, communism will be the first to go. It will be wiped off the face of this earth. Capitalism will also disappear some time later, leaving no trace."

Harisadhan commented in a mildly challenging tone, "Baba, what is happening is just the opposite of what you are saying. Communism is spreading all over the world."

"Wait for a few more years. It will disappear before your very eyes," replied Baba.

A few days later Baba told Kishun Singh that communist rule would disappear first from the European countries and then gradually from China. It would take some time for it to be rooted out of China, but it was sure to happen.

During his darshan the following Sunday, the 2nd of February 1958, Baba announced the formation of the Renaissance Artists and Writers Association (RAWA), saying that it would be an adjunct to Renaissance Universal and that its purpose would be to infuse new life into literature and the arts. It had five sub-sections covering the most important of the fine arts: the Artists and Painters Association, the Dramatists and Cinema-Artists Association, the Musicians and Dancers Association, the Writers Association and the Journalists Association.

About a year earlier, on the 14th of February 1957, Baba had started dictating on a topic entitled 'The Practice of Art and Literature.' It was a long treatise in which he explained the real objective of literature. Literature is not the portrayal of the superficial side of social life, nor is it the colorful spell of fantasy. Rather it is the portrait of real life, an external expression of the internal workings of the mind, a bold and powerful expression of the suppressed sighs of the human heart. In order to preserve the sanctity and prestige of its name, literature must reflect the dynamic currents of society.

"The word *sahitya*, loosely translated as literature, can be interpreted as *sa* + *hita* = *hitenasaha*, 'that which co-exists with *hita* [welfare]'. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term *sahitya*.

"..... Literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement 'Art for art's sake' is not acceptable; rather we should say, 'Art for service and blessedness.'"

Baba went on to discuss the social responsibility of an artist or writer. He discussed drama, poetry, short stories, children's literature, painting and the other arts. He also

introduced two new categories of literature – epochal, relating to a particular age, and leading to the transcendental realm.

Baba inspired artists not to be afraid of struggle to present the truth even in the face of opposition and persecution. He declared, "The thought of public welfare alone should be the guiding force behind all artistic and literary creation, and that thought will express itself only through artistic joy. Only then can the subtle intellect awaken in crude minds.

"So when artists or *sahityikas* have to create such a flow of delight as they move forward, they cannot afford to cling to any fastidious notions of so-called purity or impurity, for this will retard their progress. Excessive prudery will obstruct their movement. Conservative writers will compose poems about the sea, mountains and moonlight; they will paint literary pictures of the drawing-rooms of the aristocratic Ballygunge [wealthy locality in Calcutta] elite, but it will offend their pens to write about the endless humiliations, the low standard of living and primitive nature of the neglected, uneducated society in the villages, because these matters are unpleasant. The abominable life of corrupt women, the obnoxious environment of the slums, the carnal cravings of antisocial human beasts – all these they seek to avoid because they are unacceptable to their standards of 'decency' and 'decorum'.

"Here it must be noted that artists must seek to exhibit to people the simple form of truth, sweetened with the tenderness of their hearts. But it is a matter of great regret that there is a class of modern artists, who in the realms of poetry, novels, cinema, drama, etc., employ all their artistic talents for the sole purpose of kindling people's crude sensuality instead of portraying human propensities with the idealistic outlook of a true artist – what to speak of portraying their subtler human feelings. Without supporting conservatism, I would say that this class of artists is truly a blot on society."

In this long treatise on art and literature, Baba emphasized that every artistic expression should always bear in mind that guiding the entire humanity towards the transcendental goal is the true purpose of any art form.

He concluded with an ardent appeal to writers across the planet:

"Today not even the Pacific Ocean between Asia and America is difficult to cross. The people of Asia and America are touching each other's minds and have learned to accept each other empathetically as their own. Europe, Africa, Australia, Mercury, Jupiter, the stars, the comets, the constellations – none of them is alien to the other; none is distant from the other. Gradually everyone has begun to realize the vibration of the one Universal Mind.

"It is my firm conviction that the future of humanity is not dark. Every human being will reach that inextinguishable flame that is forever alight beyond the veil of the darkness of the present – and reach it they must. Those who carry the message of that effulgent light will be forever revered by all humanity. I see in the writers and artists of today the potential to become such memorable and venerable people, and that is why I hold them in high regard."

Baba's aim in founding RAWA was far-reaching. He saw artists and writers as catalysts that would help to build the pillars of a new society based on higher human values. Owing to their special talents they have the ability to shape the thinking of the general masses, and to awaken in people a universal outlook and the thirst for a society based on moral and spiritual values.

One day during his Field Walk Baba explained to Asthana another role of RAWA - to neutralize the negative influence of pseudo-culture on society. He remarked, "In the future pseudo-culture will be a great threat to humanity. It will propel people towards total degeneration. RAWA will have to rescue everyone from the debasing influence of pseudo-culture."

Baba devoted much time to translating his literary ideas into a tangible form that artists and litterateurs could use to inspire society towards higher ideals. In this way he contributed immensely to the field of literature, philology, linguistics and music. Through these wide-

ranging contributions, he has tremendously increased the scope of human expression in diverse fields and laid the foundation for a global cultural renaissance.

From March 1958 onwards Baba dictated to Sunil Chatterjee many new and interesting ideas relating to social, economic and other topical issues. These thoughts were later published in a book entitled *Problem of the Day*. Baba also expanded on the revolutionary concept of Cosmic Inheritance, which he had first propounded in the Trimohan DMC discourse.

Baba's words sum up the deeper meaning of this intriguing concept: "The principle of Cosmic Inheritance is based on the idea of the Cosmic Family, which implies the common origin and interdependence of everything in the universe, both animate and inanimate. All living beings, including animals and plants, are therefore joint owners of all the resources of the universe and have an equal right to utilize them according to their needs."

This seminal discourse created a seismic shift from a worldview that is based on personal interest to one that is universal in outlook, and considers the entire universe and its inhabitants as a single, large, universal family. Baba named this universal family *Ananda Parivara*, meaning blissful family. The principle of Cosmic Inheritance later became the cornerstone of the Ananda Marga socio-economic philosophy.

Baba repeatedly stressed that the collective social body would have to ensure everyone's right to food, water, clothes, shelter, medical treatment and education. He explained that if these basic needs were not adequately met, the concept of the collective welfare of humanity would remain an empty slogan and there would be a grave danger of moral degeneration.

Baba also made another important point. At a time when the powerful, developed nations were plundering the resources of the weaker, underdeveloped countries, he pointed out that any form of nationalism would inevitably result in one country becoming wealthy at the expense of the others. This type of mentality was the result of a certain type of psychic disease. From the perspective of an indivisible human family, such a mentality is highly detrimental to all-round human welfare. Nationalism as a form of governance is by definition the antithesis of the concept of a single, undivided human family.

Baba put forward another revolutionary idea with a view to closing some loopholes in the political system. He proposed that all electoral candidates should be required to write a manifesto, which would serve as their contract with the electorate. Violations of this agreement or any part of it could then be challenged in a court of law by the electorate and, if found guilty, the politician in question could lose his or her seat.

Baba also discussed the need for a wider governance structure beyond the boundaries of the nation state in order to materialize his vision of one indivisible human family. This thinking crystallised into the concept of a benevolent world government with the authority to uphold the basic rights of every human being on the planet.

He remarked, "With advances in technology, people's mastery over space and time will gradually increase; as a result they will feel a profound need for a world government. Every atom and molecule of this universe is the common property of all living beings. This has to be recognized as a matter of principle. After recognizing this fact, statements such as, 'This is indigenous and that is foreign, so-and-so is qualified for the citizenship of such-and-such a country while others are not', and 'Such-and-such community will get certain political rights', will become totally unacceptable. In fact, such statements nakedly expose the vested interests of certain groups of people. When the people of one country suffer due to the lack of land or food while those of another have abundant land and plentiful food, what else is it but a form of capitalism?"

Expanding on the theme of global governance, Baba said, "All people have the right to travel and settle anywhere and everywhere they like and live as dignified human beings. This is their birthright. If a certain group of people in any country refuses to accept this fundamental human right of other human beings, it is to be understood that their slogans of

peace are bogus and are only intended to hoodwink people. What to speak of this tiny earth, every planet, satellite, star, meteor and galaxy is the homeland of human beings!"

He also drew attention to the narrow sentiments that make it difficult to establish a world government and said, "The more magnanimous or expanded the human mind becomes, the more it rises above the sentiments of tribalism, communalism, provincialism and so forth. Often I hear people say that nationalism is an appreciable sentiment and that it is devoid of narrowness. But is that true? Nationalism is also relative, just like tribalism, communalism or provincialism.

"Those who want to promote the welfare of the entire human race must remain above all parochial sentiments. They have no alternative but to embrace universalism with their heart and soul; there is no other way. If everyone is looked upon as one's own, no one remains outside one's family. This naturally leaves no scope for conflict, envy or narrowness."

Baba not only talked generally about such a society of the future, he also made certain startling predictions. For instance, during the dictation of his book *Problem of the Day*, he made a forecast that in the future babies would be created in laboratories, as human beings would lose their capacity to reproduce biologically. This was indeed a remarkable prediction that was beyond the imagination of most people at that time.

Baba concluded his first social treatise by stressing two points that would play a crucial role in leading human beings towards the final goal of supreme fulfilment – benevolent intellect and unity. He reminded right-thinking people that reading voluminous treatises on philosophy would be of little use in awakening the benevolent intellect and suggested that it could only be awakened if a person sincerely followed the moral principles of *yama-niyama*. On the second point of establishing social unity, he urged people to adopt an ideology that elevated their minds above all spatial, temporal and personal differences – a cosmic ideology that would be the polestar of their lives and lead them to the understanding that really "we are all citizens of this vast universe."

# CHAPTER 26

# The Golden Hill

As the Marga entered its fourth year, it started to spread rapidly in every nook and corner of Bihar. It also attracted large numbers of followers in the nearby state of Bengal, the Northeast, as well as northern and central India. As an increasing number of people were initiated, some were trained as acharyas. Every acharya was expected to periodically take leave from work and go to different areas to propagate the Marga's ideals. The other Margis helped the visiting acharyas by arranging meetings and group discussions for them. Although the ideology and spiritual practices of the Marga attracted newcomers, they were captivated more by Baba's radiant personality, and it was this feature that brought them closer to the Marga.

The Margis who came to Jamalpur to see Baba faced two kinds of scrutiny. The first was regarding their adherence to the spiritual practice and moral principles, and the other was about the work they had accomplished to spread the ideology of the Marga.

### Intervention in a Caste Debate

From his early days, Baba had vowed to put an end to the caste system. So from the very inception of Ananda Marga, he made it a condition that anyone wanting to take initiation should first renounce all caste insignia. He never tolerated any type of caste feeling in his disciples. One incident that happened in the middle of 1958 clearly demonstrated how implacable Baba's opposition to the caste system was.

One summer afternoon, Harinarayan Sahu, a relatively new disciple, was defending the caste system in a discussion with Acharya Dipanarayan in the jagrti. He said that since the caste system had been in vogue for several millennia and had been sanctioned by the scriptures, nobody should question it. Dipanarayan animatedly opposed this view. Both of them quoted from the scriptures in support of their arguments. Although he agreed with Dipanarayan's logic, Harinarayan contended that even though the caste system was illogical and not supported by scientific facts, it would be difficult to abandon this tradition which had been practiced for hundreds of generations. He asserted that even Ananda Marga would not be able to remove the caste feeling from society, no matter how hard it tried. Both were deeply entrenched in defending their own view of the issue, while a few onlookers listened to them with great interest.

Suddenly, an excited cry went up, "Baba is coming," instantly drawing everyone's attention. They were all surprised to see Baba coming to the jagrti at that unusual hour. Moreover, he was clad only in a lungi instead of more formal attire. Everyone stood up and greeted him. With a grim look on his face, Baba directed all of them to come to his room. Once they had taken their seats, Baba spoke in an angry tone, "When I conceived Ananda Marga years ago, I vowed that I would do everything required to eradicate the caste system and other discriminatory practices that divide society. So it disturbs me very much to hear one of my own disciples justifying the existence of the caste system. I was taking some rest in this unbearable heat when I overheard your conversation. I could not keep quiet and that is why I have rushed over here." Then turning to Harinarayan he continued, "Harinarayan, castes are not ordained by God. They have been created and perpetuated by some people to suppress and exploit the others. Those scriptures that you quoted to justify the caste system were created by the same people. A true lover of God cannot support any kind of division or discrimination among human beings no matter how deeply rooted it is. Do you know how much pain the socially oppressed suffer due to caste prejudice? I can hear the cries of agony of those downtrodden human beings. That is why I have taken a vow to destroy the caste system, and no force on this earth can stop me from doing so."

Everyone was taken aback by Baba's forceful words and the tone in which he uttered them. Harinarayan fell at Baba's feet begging for forgiveness and promised never again to support the caste system.

### Tripathi's Ego Humbled

After becoming an acharya, Amulyaratan wanted to take up some of the programs that Baba had newly introduced to spread the ideals of the Marga. When he heard about Tattvasabha as a new method of spreading the Marga's philosophy among the public at large, he planned a large program in the sub-divisional town of Ramnagar in Champaran, North Bihar in June 1958. He thought that it would be insufficient to give only intellectual food to the people. The poor and the hungry would have no interest in elaborate philosophical discussions about Ananda Marga. He therefore decided to organize a *Narayan seva*, another program given by Baba to provide free food to the poor as a service to the poverty-stricken masses. So he decided to organize a combined program—a Narayan Seva to serve lunch to the poor people, and in the evening a philosophical discussion for the general public. As he was the highest-ranking government officer in the subdivision and was highly respected for his honesty and integrity, there was great enthusiasm among the townspeople to learn more about the Ananda Marga philosophy.

However, he faced some difficulties in finding a suitable location for the Tattvasabha. The only appropriate place for holding such a large program was the Premjanani Sanskrit High School. However, there was a problem. Kamalakant Tripathi, the founder and principal of the school, was a dogmatic Brahmin who had a massive superiority complex because of his high caste and erudition. He nursed a deep dislike for Ananda Marga due to its rejection of the caste system. As Tripathi was hostile to Ananda Marga, Amulyaratan wondered how to persuade him to allow the Tattvasabha to be held in his institution. One day Tripathi came to Amulyaratan's office for some official work. Taking a chance, Amulyaratan broached the subject of the Tattvasabha.

"Tripathiji, we want to organize a symposium on philosophy for the public, and you are an excellent speaker. So I would like you to preside over the program and, unless you have any objection, I would also like your permission to hold the program in your school premises."

Surprisingly, Tripathi readily consented to both requests. It was only after he left that Amulyaratan started to feel a disturbing disquiet about his choice of Tripathi as president of the conference, a decision he had made on the spur of the moment. He was worried that Tripathi would ruin the impact created by the Marga speakers by using his presidential speech to denounce their views. As the person presiding over the meeting, Tripathi would be the last to speak. This would place the Margi speakers in a disadvantaged position as they would not have the opportunity to respond to any confusion created by him.

Amulyaratan invited two senior acharyas to present the Ananda Marga philosophy—Sakaldev Singh and Ramtanuk Singh, both of them lawyers and excellent orators. Sukhadev Paswan, a Margi officer in the Welfare Department, was entrusted with the task of finding about a hundred of the most indigent people for the feeding program.

Sukhadev, a very devoted but simple-minded person, asked the leaders of one of the villages where he was doing development work to send some of the poorest villagers for lunch at the house of the deputy collector, but he omitted to specify the exact number. When the villagers turned up, Amulyaratan was shocked. Over two hundred people came, more than twice the number for whom food had been prepared. He was at a loss as to what to do.

"What can I do now?" he wondered. "When so many people have come how can I insult them by not giving them a full meal? Baba has said, 'Those whom you are serving should be treated as God. It is not you who are obliging needy people by serving them; rather you should be grateful to the Lord for giving you the chance to serve Him through those needy

human beings. So you should treat those who come to take service from you as the representatives of the Lord Himself.’”

“Something must be done immediately,” he decided.

While he was giving instructions to make arrangements to cook more food, which would take two to three hours, Sukhadev complicated matters further by starting to serve the food, and all the villagers sat down to eat.

Amulyaratan was now in a quandary. He did not know how to extricate himself from the problems created by Sukhadev. In desperation, he closed his eyes and mentally beseeched Baba, “Baba, with great sincerity I have prepared everything for the mass feeding. Matters have taken an unexpected turn, and now there is only sufficient food for less than half the number of people who have come in response to our invitation. Kindly save me from the sin of insulting these hungry people by feeding them only half a meal, for that would also be an insult to you, and I cannot bear to even think about that.”

Amulyaratan surrendered the problem to Baba and sat down to meditate. After a while, when he came out to see what was happening, he was amazed at what he saw. After taking only a small quantity of food, the guests said that they were full. In fact, when Ramtanuk and Sukhadev went around asking them if they wanted a second helping, they declined. Amulyaratan couldn’t believe his eyes. He himself asked a few people if they wanted a second helping. They too declined, saying that their stomachs were full.

Amulyaratan and his entire team were baffled by the incredible phenomenon of how all the people felt satisfied after eating only half belly. He then realized that Baba had intervened to save them from an embarrassing situation. Amulyaratan’s eyes filled with tears as he thought how Baba’s gracious intervention had solved his predicament and how he had been saved from a major embarrassment.

More surprises were in store for him later in the day. That evening the gathering at the Tattvasabha was huge, far beyond the Margis’ expectations.

After Tripathi and the speakers took their seats at the podium, Amulyaratan welcomed everyone with a brief introductory speech. Next to speak was Sakaldev Singh, who spoke with great conviction about “Today’s problems and the solutions offered by Ananda Marga.” He explained logically how the caste sentiment was destroying the social fabric of India and how vested interests had been propagating the idea that the caste system was created by God. He forcefully rebutted this belief by quoting the part of the Gita where Lord Krishna said that God had created four classes in accordance with people’s different psychologies and the type of work they performed. Sakaldev then drove home the point that these psychologies should not be confused or equated with hereditary castes, which, he asserted, were the product of an exploitative social system.

He concluded by suggesting that meditation was one of the highest forms of worship, while by contrast, idol worship was the most inferior form, supporting his arguments by quoting from the Tantras.

In a society steeped in dogma and caste sentiments, such ideas were radical. Nevertheless, everyone listened with rapt attention and at the end applauded his presentation. Seeing the enthusiastic public endorsement of these radical ideas, Tripathi’s face turned red, and he was visibly ill at ease. Amulyaratan then invited Ramtanuk to take questions from the floor. Several questions were asked and Ramtanuk deftly fielded all of them. Meanwhile Tripathi appeared to be restless and kept muttering under his breath that he would give a fitting reply to every point the Margis raised when his turn came to speak.

Finally, the time came for him to deliver the president’s concluding speech. His facial expression clearly showed that he was very upset by what the two acharyas had said and was itching to attack their views. Amulyaratan was very concerned that he might ruin the positive impact of their speeches and rued his decision to invite such a hostile person to preside over the function. As Tripathi got up to speak, Amulyaratan closed his eyes and mentally prayed to

Baba, "Baba, time and again, you have come to my rescue. Once again I am pleading with you not to allow Tripathi to spoil the good atmosphere created by the two acharyas." As he implored Baba mentally, he felt Baba telling him, "Don't feel disturbed. The Supreme Being always supports your efforts to serve others."

Strangely, just as he finished requesting Baba to intervene, he heard an elderly woman's voice speaking in Hindi, "So far I have kept quiet and have restrained myself with great difficulty. But now I can keep quiet no longer."

The verbs he used were in the feminine form. Hearing this, the entire audience started to boo and laugh at the speaker. Amulyaratan opened his eyes to see what was happening, curious to know who this woman was who had invited the public's derision. To his surprise, instead of a woman, he saw Tripathi standing in front of the microphone with a perplexed look on his face, as the booing continued. His face was ashen, and he was sweating in the cool evening breeze. As the booing continued, he sat down unable to utter a single word in the infuriating din. Amulyaratan was completely astounded at what had transpired. As the jeering and booing continued unabated, Tripathi abruptly signalled the end of the symposium and left the place in a huff.

After everyone became quiet, Amulyaratan asked Ramtanuk, "What actually happened? I was very worried about the damaging speech that Tripathiji was about to give, and was meditating on Baba when the booing started."

"It is not very clear to me either," replied Ramtanuk. "Tripathiji got up and started to speak. But his voice sounded like that of a woman and he used feminine verb endings, and then everyone started to boo and jeer at him. How could such a scholarly person do such a silly thing?"

"Whatever the reason may be, I am glad that he was unable to cause any disturbance. It was worrying me very much," replied Amulyaratan with a sigh of deep relief.

Several people showed interest in learning meditation, and Amulyaratan was very pleased that the Tattvasabha had been quite successful.

When Ramtanuk went to Jamalpur some days later, Baba casually asked him during the evening Field Walk, "Ramtanuk, how was the program in Ramnagar?"

"By your grace, everything went very well, Baba. The response was very good and many people were initiated, including many youths."

"I hope there was no shortage of food," said Baba with a mysterious smile. Ramtanuk then described how they had been saved from a big embarrassment.

"Do you know what actually happened?"

Ramtanuk remained silent waiting for Baba to clear up the mystery. Baba clarified, "Due to his carelessness, Sukhadev botched up the mass feeding program. Amulya was very worried that many of the poor people who had been invited would have to return home hungry. Whatever happened was not Amulya's mistake. So I instructed Nature to rescue him from the difficult situation. There was an immediate change in the people's metabolic system and they all felt satisfied after eating very little food."

"We too felt that it was a miracle because village people normally take more than twice the amount of food we eat," said Ramtanuk.

"And what did that Kamalakant Tripathi say?" Baba asked with a smile.

"He couldn't say anything. He committed some strange mistakes and the public started to jeer."

"No, Ramtanuk, Tripathi didn't commit any mistake. He was made to do it. Do you want to know the secret of what actually happened? When he heard you and Sakaldev speak against the traditional ideas of the caste system and ritualistic worship, he became very upset and wanted to attack your views and confuse the public during his address. Amulya was worried that all the efforts to organize such a big program would go to waste if Tripathi condemned your speeches. As he was the last speaker there wouldn't have been any chance for further

clarification after that. So, I created a small change in his mind as well as his vocal cord. For a short time he felt as if he was a woman and that made him use feminine verbs. With the change in his vocal cord, the pitch of his voice changed and it sounded like a woman's voice."

Saying this Baba laughed heartily and the others joined in. Baba then continued, "Although he has done the public immense good by starting the Sanskrit school, he actually needed such a lesson because he had a very bloated ego about his knowledge of the scriptures and Sanskrit. He would behave arrogantly with people and never missed a chance to flaunt his bookish knowledge. He thought he could easily outwit you both and confuse the public with his knowledge and his eloquence. But he could not even complete the first line. Even now, Tripathi is confused about what happened to him and why he made such a strange and embarrassing error."

Ramtanuk realized that these incidents that had baffled them all were actually Baba's divine intervention.

### Spiritual Urge in a Criminal Lawyer

Advocate Pratapaditya Tripathi belonged to a reputed family from a village near Gorakhpur. He took initiation from Acharya Raghunath in mid-1958. His first darshan of the guru was in July of the same year when Baba went to Gorakhpur to hold a DMC. However, Pratapaditya was hardly able to have any contact with Baba at that time. Some months later, he went to Jamalpur. During that visit he gained a better understanding about the guru. Years later, during his interview, he recalled his experiences:

> While Baba was in Gorakhpur, the only opportunity I got to see him at close quarters was when my acharya formally introduced me to him. Other than that, I only saw him from a distance during the General Darshan in the mornings and evenings. After attending his first discourse, I began to feel an inexplicable ecstasy arising within me. That feeling gradually increased during Baba's stay and created in me an intense attraction for the guru. I felt a strong urge to see him again, and within a few weeks I went to Jamalpur for a couple of days with my acharya. During the darshan in the Jamalpur jagrti, I was sitting in the back row. The first thing that Baba asked was who had come to Jamalpur for the first time. I stood up. Although I had been briefly introduced to him in Gorakhpur, I thought that he might have forgotten me. So I again introduced myself, saying, "I am Pratapaditya. I have come from Gorakhpur."
>
> Baba smiled and asked, "Are you really from Gorakhpur?"
>
> "Yes Baba. I am from Gorakhpur."
>
> "Are you originally from Gorakhpur town? Is your house in Gorakhpur?"
>
> "Yes Baba. I am from Gorakhpur town."
>
> "No, I have just scanned the entire town of Gorakhpur. I don't see your home anywhere in Gorakhpur."
>
> Baba's statement was a bit puzzling, but there was some truth in what he said.
>
> I corrected myself, "I live there in a rented house. But my original home is in a village near Gorakhpur."
>
> I withheld the name of the village, thinking that Baba would not know about my tiny village.
>
> "Yes, it's in that small village of Vishvanathpur, isn't it?"
>
> I was taken aback. I thought, "How does Baba know the name of my village when it is not even known in Gorakhpur?"
>
> In fact, throughout the whole area our village is known as "Saria", although Saria is actually a large village adjacent to our small village.
>
> Baba then added to my surprise by asking, "Yes, isn't your house the big one with a large pit on each side?"

As I wondered how he knew all this, Baba looked at me intently. That mysterious look gave me the feeling that he knew not only about my village but in fact everything about me from my childhood, and that he had been watching me since my birth. I felt that my relationship with him was not from this life alone but that we had been connected for several lives.

Echoing my feeling Baba said, "Your relationship with me is not from this life alone. It started several lives ago."

I spent the rest of my stay in Jamalpur savoring the realization that my guru was not an ordinary guru, but an all-knowing entity in the true sense.

The next evening we were due to return to Gorakhpur, and our train was scheduled to leave just before 10 pm. My acharya and I went with Baba to the Tiger's Grave during his evening Field Walk. At the Tiger's Grave, Baba was talking to my acharya and some others who were with us, and the discussion continued for a long time. Ten o'clock was fast approaching and I became restless, as we were sure to miss the train if we delayed any further. But I felt it would be impolite to interrupt Baba's talk. I kept signalling to my acharya that we should hurry, but he ignored me.

At half past ten, Baba suddenly cut short his discussion and said, "Raghunath, don't you have a train to catch tonight? I think you should leave now without any further delay."

On this cue, we prostrated before Baba and took our leave. We picked up our luggage that we had left near the Englishman's grave and walked quickly towards the railway station. On the way I suggested to Raghunathji, "Acharyaji, we are sure to miss the train. So let us go back to the jagrti and take a train the next morning instead."

He pacified me, "Baba knew exactly when the train would arrive and had delayed us on purpose. Didn't you realize who your guru is in yesterday's darshan? So don't worry about missing the train. He won't let the train leave without us."

I was unable to comprehend that such worldly matters like the movement of a train could be controlled by the spiritual power of a guru. To pacify my restless mind, Raghunathji heeded my pleas to hurry.

When we finally reached the station, both of us were totally drained of energy and were gasping for breath. We were unable to walk even a few steps more out of sheer exhaustion. Somehow we staggered onto the platform to discover that our train was about to arrive. I raced off to buy the tickets, and just as I returned, it pulled in. I was amazed that Baba had asked us to leave at exactly the right moment, perfectly synchronising our arrival at the station with the arrival of the train, not a minute sooner and not a minute later.

We boarded the train and lay down on a couple of empty berths. As the train slowly pulled away from the platform, my mind wandered back down memory lane and my earliest spiritual impulses flashed across my mind.

Since my adolescence, I used to have an intense desire to do sadhana, and that desire had attracted me to many spiritual gatherings. But what I heard at those programs did not satisfy my rational mind. I had also experimented with a variety of spiritual practices, but none of them could quench my spiritual thirst. So I felt a spiritual vacuum in my life, even as I completed my law studies and embarked on the professional life of a criminal lawyer. After joining this profession, I lost whatever hope I ever had of gaining spiritual fulfilment, which had been my deepest dream. I thought that my spiritual longing would remain unfulfilled, and that created a feeling of deep discontent in my life.

One day Satchidanandji, an honorary magistrate in the Gorakhpur court, remarked, "Pratapaditya, I have been observing you closely. I feel that maybe you are a misfit in this kind of profession."

I was surprised at his unexpected comment. I had been very successful as a criminal lawyer since the early days of my professional life, so why did he think that I was a misfit?

He continued, "Although you are a successful lawyer and have impressed all the judges with your skills, I see that you are an introverted person, of a type we generally don't find in this profession."

I admitted that I had searched but had failed to find a spiritual guru. He then talked to me about Ananda Marga, but I was not completely convinced. He urged me to contact Acharya Raghunath, but his exposition of Ananda Marga philosophy also failed to impress me. However, after talking to both of them, I understood that there was a deep philosophy behind Ananda Marga that neither of them was able to explain properly. So I asked for some literature, and Satchidanandji gave me *Subhashita Samgraha Part 1*, the book containing Baba's earliest DMC discourses. As I read it, my desire to know more about Ananda Marga philosophy intensified, and I decided to miss the court that day so that I could continue reading the fascinating book. In it I found a new interpretation of spirituality which corresponded to what I had been searching for. As I read, for some unknown reason tears occasionally welled up in my eyes. The concluding lines of one particular discourse captivated me beyond measure:

> "O human beings, you are fortunate. The clarion call of the Universal Entity has reached you. Not only has the call come but you are hearing it, and it is vibrating in every cell of your body. Will you now lie inert in a corner of your house and waste your time clinging to and bemoaning old skeletons? The Supreme Being is calling you in the roar of the ocean, in the thunder of the clouds, in the flash of the lightning, in the meteor's flaming fires. Nothing will come from sitting idle. Get up and awaken the clouded chivalry of your dormant youth. It may be that the path is not strewn with flowers and that an inferiority complex will attempt to hold down your advancing steps, but even then, you must proceed onwards, tearing the shroud of darkness. You will pierce through the thick darkness of despair as you race forward in your chariot, radiant with the sun's brilliance, towards the attainment of the supreme state."

I felt that through these lines the guru was giving me the call for which I had been waiting in anguish all these years. I read those few lines again and again. I knew that I had found my path and decided not to delay any further. That evening I contacted Satchidanandji, and he asked me to meet Acharya Raghunath for initiation.

Keeping pace with the train, my thoughts moved forward as I ruminated over how I had finally met the guru, and I don't know when I fell asleep.

### Bargaining With the Guru

Another initiate from Gorakhpur had a very different experience. A few months after his first visit to Jamalpur, Pratapaditya again accompanied Baba during his evening Field Walk. Satchidananda and a new local initiate of his were also among those present. This newcomer was a very rich man and the owner of one of the largest publishing houses in India which disseminated religious and spiritual books. After hearing about Baba's miraculous powers, he expressed a strong desire to meet the guru. Unlike the other Margis, he had a special purpose in coming to see Baba, which he did not disclose even to his acharya. After hearing about Baba's ability to demonstrate various kinds of samadhi, he harbored a desire to experience them himself.

After Baba and the Margis took their seats on the Tiger's Grave, he waited for an appropriate moment to express his cherished desire to Baba. Baba began to talk about the Marga's activities in the Gorakhpur area. Gradually the newcomer grew impatient, wondering

when he would get the chance to make his special request to Baba. When his acharya finally introduced him to Baba, he seized the opportunity to make the request. "Baba, I have dedicated my entire life to the spread of Dharma. My publishing company is the most famous company in India for the distribution of spiritual books. We have helped to spread the message of the Bhagavat Gita far and wide. I would also like to help to spread the books of Ananda Marga, and can promote the Marga publications in a big way."

Baba said, "Oh, I see. It is good that you are doing so much to spread spiritual teachings. It is also good that you want to spread our Marga books through your publications company. You can talk to the general secretary about it. I don't handle those matters."

Not satisfied with Baba's response, he continued, "Baba, I also want to financially support the service projects of the Marga. I can also help to spread Dharma in the entire country. My book stalls are all over the country."

"All these things too you can discuss with the general secretary," replied Baba curtly.

"Baba, I have been doing so much for the spread of Dharma and I have been leading the life of a dharmic person. But I have one desire that has remained unfulfilled. For years, I have had a strong desire to experience *nirvikalpa samadhi* about which I have heard a lot. I have a small request. Kindly grace me with the experience of the highest of all samadhis – nirvikalpa samadhi."

Satchidananda was taken aback to hear his initiate trying to negotiate with Baba for the highest spiritual experience. He became apprehensive about the consequences his request might have. Baba might become angry with him as well for bringing such an initiate. After a short pause, Baba started on a mild note. "So you want to experience nirvikalpa samadhi?"

"Yes Baba, if you can kindly grace me." The newcomer became hopeful that Baba would grant him his wish.

"First, tell me if publishing spiritual books is the only yardstick for gauging a person's adherence to the principles of Dharma."

There was no response from the newcomer.

"You have been popularising the Bhagavat Gita. Tell me, what are the principles of the Bhagavat Gita that you have been following in your own life?"

Again there was no response.

Baba continued after a short pause, "Printing the Gita and other spiritual books and selling them for profit does not make you a follower of Dharma. What you are doing is business with a view to making money. In the process, what immoral means have you not resorted to in order to increase your wealth? How many people have you cheated, hiding behind the veneer of the fake dharmic image you have created for yourself and which you have used to amass wealth?"

The pitch of Baba's voice was gradually rising. He then recounted several examples of the newcomer's immoral business deals and described in detail how he had cheated various people, mentioning their names and the places where these deals occurred, and other details as well. He continued relentlessly exposing many more of the man's moral failings. When the newcomer asked for the experience of nirvikalpa samadhi, he had not bargained for the scrutiny of a guru who would openly expose the dark hidden aspects of his personality.

At the end of a long list of disclosures Baba asked, "Do you want me to give further details of your true character that you have been hiding from others? With all these defects, how audacious you are to ask for the experience of nirvikalpa samadhi! Spirituality is not a commodity to be sold in the marketplace. Spiritual experiences can be gained only by those who strive very hard for them and not by an immoral person like you."

Baba turned to Satchidananda and asked, "Why did you bring such an immoral person to me? Do you think that his influence and wealth will help the growth of Ananda Marga? If I want, I can even turn the vast Himalayas into gold in the twinkling of an eye. Look at Kali Pahar," Baba ordered pointing to the hill on his left.

Everyone was taken aback to see that the entire hill had turned into gold and was glittering in the faint moonlight.

Then turning back to the newcomer, Baba asked, "Do you have more wealth than this that you can use to buy nirvikalpa samadhi? Do you want to buy me like you buy others?"

The Margis were stunned by what Baba had said and shown. It seemed as if his voice was reverberating through the entire field, and their whole being was vibrating with an intense devotional thrill. The businessman turned pale and fumbled for words. He apologized and begged for forgiveness.

Lowering his voice Baba continued, "You will become eligible for nirvikalpa samadhi when your attraction for the Lord becomes a million times more intense than the attraction you feel towards worldly things like wealth, name, fame, power, and position."

Baba paused for a while and continued, "I know this will be an impossible task for you, so I am asking you to do something that is possible. I guarantee you the experience of nirvikalpa samadhi if you do just a few things. First, return the money to all the people you have cheated and genuinely repent your actions. Then, you must strictly follow the principles of yama-niyama and do your sadhana twice daily as per the system for a period of one year. If you succeed in doing what I have asked you to do, you may come to me after a year and I will fulfil your desire to experience nirvikalpa samadhi."

The businessman assured Baba that he would follow his instructions. He appeared eager to leave as quickly as possible. On their return to town, upon reaching the railway station, he excused himself telling Satchidananda that he had to catch a train. The rest of the Margis continued walking with Baba as far as his Keshavpur residence.

Before Baba entered his house, he said, "When this man came to Jamalpur, even in his wildest dreams he never anticipated that he would get such treatment. He had expected that he would get the same warm welcome that he has been accustomed to receiving whenever he visited ashrams and sadhus. He is not used to the kind of discomfiture that he experienced today, and it will be hard for him to digest it. That is why he left so abruptly, even though there is no train tonight. Satchidananda, this is the last time he will want to have any contact with Ananda Marga. You should not try to contact him either. The Marga has nothing to gain from such immoral people who are only after name, fame, and wealth and are unwilling to be reformed."

With these words Baba took his leave and slowly walked into his house. The Margis continued to stand there for a while, trying to relive the bliss of that evening's occurrence, before slowly walking back to the Rampur Colony jagrti.

### Baba's Modest Lifestyle

Even though the number of disciples started to grow rapidly and many of them were highly placed government officers or well-to-do businessmen, Baba's lifestyle remained very simple. He never allowed the Margis to bring him gifts or food or anything material despite their eagerness to do so. Frustrated by his consistent refusals, they came to a consensus that "this guru takes only one thing from us and that too in great abundance, and that is our sins which he takes without our permission or even our knowledge." Sometimes different Margis mentioned this to Baba in a tone of exasperation but Baba simply laughed it off.

Baba's family somehow managed on the meager salaries he and Kanai brought home, a third of which they set aside for the maintenance of the family of his elder sister, Hiraprabha. She had become a widow in February 1950, when her husband Ramani Mohan Basu passed away at the early age of forty-five. Another part of the family income was spent on the education of his two youngest brothers, Himanshu and Manas. Baba never went to collect his salary, leaving that duty to Kanai, who handed it over to Mother Abharani. From it she gave two rupees to Baba as pocket money. He spent part of that on garlands and sweets that Abharani needed for the worship of the gods on special occasions. At the end of the month, he

handed over whatever remained unspent to his mother. His disciples and colleagues sometimes saw him wearing torn clothes that had been mended by Abharani. Some close colleagues asked Baba why he led such a simple life when he had thousands of disciples. He gently brushed them off saying that as long as he was employed and earning a salary, he did not want to accept anything from the organization for his personal needs.

Baba left all mundane matters relating to his personal life, including buying clothes and other personal essentials, to Kanai, who was always alert to the needs of his elder brother. How totally unconcerned Baba was about his personal affairs is illustrated by one small incident. Kanai used to buy the cloth for Baba's clothing. One day Kanai requested Baba to go to the family tailor on the way to the field for his evening walk and take his measurements for a shirt. Before taking the measurement, the tailor asked, "Prabhat Babu, how long will the sleeves be? Will they be long or short?"

Baba replied, "Usually my shirts have long sleeves, but Kanai did not tell me whether this one will have long or short sleeves. It's better if you take the measurements for both and then you can sort it out with Kanai later." Rameshvar Bhaita who was with Baba at that time was surprised to see how unconcerned he was about his personal matters.

Kishun Singh well remembered the austerity of Baba's lifestyle:

> Late one night, in the winter of 1958, on our return from the evening Field Walk, I bent down to touch his feet before he went into the house. I was shocked to see that his right foot was covered in blood. I asked him what had happened.
>
> "I think that one of the nails used to repair my footwear has come loose and pierced my foot," replied Baba as if were an insignificant matter.
>
> "Baba, why didn't you tell me about it on the way?"
>
> "Kishun, I was so engrossed in your company that I didn't notice it."
>
> With tears in my eyes I pleaded, "Baba, please allow me to buy you a pair of sandals or other shoes of your choice tomorrow."
>
> "No Kishun, that is not necessary. I will ask Kanai to get it repaired again. Then it can last for several more months."[^1]
>
> With these words Baba blessed me and disappeared into the house despite my repeated protests. I couldn't check my tears as I walked back to my residence.

On another occasion I went inside his room. The only things there were a simple cot which he shared with his brother, Kanai, a suitcase containing his clothes, and a couple of hangers where the clothing he wore to go out was hanging. It was a hot summer day, and the room was extremely hot. The only means of cooling the air was a hand-fan. Baba was a living example of the principle of *aparigraha*, which is part of yama-niyama, i.e., how to maintain one's life with only the bare essentials.

[^1]: A pair of Baba's sandals which had been repeatedly mended with many nails in them is kept in Baba's Museum in Calcutta. A disciple, Acharya Kailas Bhalla of Raipur, compelled him to part with it in exchange of a new pair during Baba's DMC visit to Raipur on 21^st^ September 1966.

CHAPTER 27

# Seeking Divine Intervention

Margis in general were keenly aware that Baba was all-knowing and that he was much better at looking after them than they were themselves. For his part, Baba reminded them on various occasions that the relationship between the disciple and the Sadguru should be based solely on devotion and completely free from expectations. So they felt that it would be inappropriate to ask for anything from him, be it spiritual or material. However, during the early days of the Marga in Jamalpur the Margis enjoyed such intimacy with Baba that they treated him more like a very close family member than as a guru. It was therefore natural for them to approach him with even their most mundane problems, big or small. In a break from the traditional guru-disciple relationship, Baba also behaved like a doting father, solving all their worldly difficulties.

"We often used to ask Baba for help with our family problems because we felt that he was the guardian of our family as well as our divine protector. He also responded in a similar manner," reminisced Acharya Vishvanath, a veterinary doctor.

He then related some memorable occasions where he approached Baba for help in resolving some of his relatives' mundane problems and how Baba obliged him despite being unhappy that he had come to him on their behalf:

Once, my cousin was arranging his daughter's marriage. After the engagement, while the preparations for the marriage were underway, an astrologer engaged by the family said that the stars of the couple were incompatible. This meant that either the boy or the girl would die soon after the marriage or some other great tragedy would befall the family.

It was very disturbing news for everyone concerned. The family elders requested me to consult Baba, but I did not want to bother him with such frivolous matters. However, the other members of the family also pressurised me to seek Baba's guidance, saying that the preparations for the marriage were in the final stage and that it was a question of the safety and security of the couple. The entire family was in turmoil. Finally, they decided that if Baba confirmed what the astrologer had said, the marriage would be called off. Left with no choice, I reluctantly agreed to go to Jamalpur.

On my arrival I went straight to Baba's residence. Upon entering his room, I prostrated before him. He immediately said with a broad smile, "So, this time my Vishvanath has come with a family problem."

I got up, did namaskar with folded hands and replied, "Baba, you know everything. You know how I have been compelled to come here against my will." I then explained in detail how I had been forced to come, although I was reluctant to do so.

"Tell me the name of the girl," Baba said.

"Her name is Munni."

"No, no! That is her nickname. What is her actual name?"

I didn't remember her actual name. We always called her by her nickname. I scratched my head, indicating that I did not know the answer.

"See, you don't even know the name of your niece. Then what have you come to inquire about? Her real name is Kamini. Now tell me the name of the boy she is going to marry."

I had no idea at all and again scratched my head. Baba then said, "His name is Vasudev Sharma. He is a lecturer in English at the local college."

I simply nodded in acknowledgement. "There is nothing to worry about the couple's future. They will have a happy life. That astrologer knows nothing."

I returned home satisfied. Baba's words were reassuring to everyone, and the marriage was solemnized as planned. As Baba had foretold, they lived a happy life together.

There was another case that I brought to Baba. My son-in-law's elder brother had been diagnosed with advanced tuberculosis. In those days there was no cure for TB, and it was considered deadly. The doctors had given up all hope. Our relatives had heard about Baba's miraculous powers, so they requested me to ask him for help. I was very reluctant to disturb Baba with such problems. But I received pressure from several quarters and finally yielded. However, I insisted on everyone taking initiation before I mentioned the matter to Baba. They all readily agreed. So when we reached Jamalpur, my relatives were initiated by Pranayda. A short while later Baba arrived at the jagrti. I went to his room and prostrated before him. While I was thinking how to broach the subject, Baba himself brought it up. "Vishvanath, you have not done the right thing. Why did you bring him here? Don't you know that his disease is in a very advanced stage?" Then pretending annoyance, he added, "You thought that if you helped them, they would become active Margis. But they have all learned meditation only to get him cured and not out of any spiritual desire. Don't make this place an asylum for sick people. If you do that, this jagrti will be flooded with the sick seeking cures for their diseases."

I felt great remorse at having disturbed Baba. He then explained the theory of samskaras and quoted a Sanskrit verse which meant that a person would have to undergo the consequences of his good and bad actions even if it took several lifetimes.

Finally he said, "The patient is suffering the reactions of his past actions. Now do you want me to go against the law of Nature?"

I didn't know what I would tell my relatives. I mentally told Baba that whatever he decided would be acceptable to me. Baba understood my predicament and said, "Alright, bring the patient here." He was too weak to stand without support and had to be assisted to walk to Baba's room. With some help he prostrated before Baba.

"Take him to the well and pour forty buckets of cold water on him," said Baba in a commanding tone. Upon hearing this, the patient and everyone else became terrified thinking that he would surely die of cold.

Baba assured them, "There is nothing to fear. Bring him here again after you have done it."

Despite everyone's misgivings, he was bathed with forty buckets of water and then brought before Baba once more.

"Make him walk unassisted to the Tiger's Grave and back non-stop," was Baba's next direction. My relatives wondered how he would accomplish such a feat, as he couldn't walk even a few steps without support. Again Baba assured them that nothing untoward would happen to him and that no one should worry about it. Then we all set out to the Tiger's Grave with the patient. Strangely, as he walked, he felt his energy increasing and on our return he said he was feeling very energetic.

When I reported this to Baba, he said, "His treatment is complete. Now take him home. He is cured."

Everyone was exhilarated to hear this news. However, I silently made a vow to never again disturb Baba with any personal or family issues. I informed all my relatives about my firm resolve. After that no one ever bothered me to seek assistance from Baba about their personal problems.

Baba's unconventional treatment appeared to be a way of creating an attitude of surrender in the patient, as forty buckets of cold water and strenuous walk could never have been the actual treatment for such a deadly disease.

In another case of tuberculosis Baba prescribed a very different course of treatment.

Ramlakhan Singh was posted in Bhagalpur as an inspector in the Central Excise and Customs Department. He was initiated by Chandranath and was actively involved in Marga work. A few years after his initiation, he developed tuberculosis. Prior to that he had enjoyed robust health, but he now became completely emaciated due to his illness. He disclosed his condition to Chandranath, saying that he was very worried, as his children were still very young and he was the sole breadwinner in his family. Chandranath was aware that Baba did not like to be disturbed with such problems. However, he had a soft spot for his initiate, who was actively working for the Marga. He therefore assured Ramlakhan that he would bring the matter to Baba's attention and seek his advice.

The next time Chandranath went to Jamalpur, he mentioned Ramlakhan's condition to Baba. "Baba, Ramlakhan and his whole family are very worried. Moreover, he is the only breadwinner in his family."

Baba closed his eyes for a while and said, "Chandranath, tell Ramlakhan that he need not worry about anything. He is not going to die of this disease. Ask him to stop all the medicines immediately. They are no use to him in his present condition. His disease has reached a very advanced stage and he cannot be cured by medicine. Teach him guru dhyana and ask him to sit for long hours in dhyana. That will be his only medicine."

After he returned to Bhagalpur, Chandranath conveyed Baba's instructions to Ramlakhan. Ramlakhan agreed to stop taking his medicine, and Chandranath taught him guru dhyana. As directed by Baba, Ramlakhan spent long hours doing meditation and soon started to improve. In a matter of days he began to recover his health and a few weeks later he was declared completely free of the disease by the doctors.

### Gracing the Faithless

Almost all the Margis had their own stories to tell about the guru, particularly about how they had received his boundless grace. Nirendra Kumar Banerjee, an employee in the Railway Workshop, was one of the early initiates. Like many others, he too had memorable experiences with Baba:

In the beginning I was the only Margi in my house. I was initiated in 1955 by Pranayda. I had two brothers. My elder brother Amarendranath Banerjee was married and was living with me. He and my sister-in-law, Kamala, were dead against Ananda Marga. Once, Kamala contracted meningitis. The doctor, who my brother consulted, advised admitting her in the hospital. So I asked him to consult another medical specialist, Dr. Dinu Haldar, who was our family doctor. He treated her for three or four days, and then, seeing no improvement, suggested admitting her in the hospital. In the Railway Hospital they gave her a thorough examination and found that she had many more complications than was originally thought. She was diagnosed with lumbago. Then she began to lose her eyesight. The medical prognosis was that she might ultimately go blind. Initially the hospital doctor had made a wrong diagnosis, so the treatment she received only aggravated her condition. It was only after Dr. Haldar examined her that the proper treatment started. She was cured of her illnesses in a few days but she lost her eyesight. Since it was not possible to treat her eyes in Jamalpur, the doctor referred her to a hospital in Patna.

In the meantime I reported the matter to Baba. He said that in Patna I would be able to get the cooperation of some Margi doctors if it was needed. Since my elder brother was unemployed, I knew that I would be expected to meet the expenses from my meager

salary, and I would not be able to afford it. I mentioned my problem to Baba and told him that it would be impossible for me to bear the financial burden of her treatment. After listening to me patiently, he instructed me to bring a red flower. I brought a red, wafer-thin bougainvillea flower from the office compound. He took the flower in his hand and closed his eyes, then handed it back to me saying, “Give it to your mother. Ask her to encase it inside an amulet and tie it around the waist of your sister-in-law. Don’t let anyone at home know that I have given this, as your brother and sister-in-law have no faith in me and are hostile to the Marga. Just say that you got it from a saint.”

I confided all this to my mother with the request that it should not be disclosed to my brother or anyone else. However, she made big news out of it. In the evening my wife and my mother went to the hospital and tied the amulet around my sister-in-law’s waist. The next morning, just as I was going to the office, I saw my elder brother returning from a visit to his wife. Upon inquiry, he said that his wife had told him that the darkness in her eyes had disappeared that morning. I was happy to hear this promising news and rushed to Baba’s office to inform him of the progress. He just smiled faintly and said that she was suffering from some other complications as well, including a female disease. He asked if she ever suffered from pleurisy. I nodded affirmatively. He also said that all her problems would be cured by the amulet and that she should keep it carefully. Then teasingly he said, “I suppose nobody abused me for giving it to her.”

My sister-in-law was fully cured within a week and was discharged. The doctor remarked that he was not sure how it had happened. I replied, “Let us think that God has performed a miracle.” The doctor nodded in agreement.

In the evening I asked my wife if my sister-in-law and brother had at least expressed their gratitude by bowing before Baba’s photo. She said, “No, they didn’t. They just commented that she had been cured due to her good fortune and by the grace of goddess Mother Kali.”

A few days later they went the Kali temple and worshipped Mother Kali. They also gave the deity an offering of a silver eye. One day after five or six months the amulet mysteriously disappeared, and no one knew how it had disappeared or where it went.
