When I reported this to Baba, he jested that the amulet had done its work and had gone away. My brother and sister-in-law knew very well that the cure had been effected only by Baba’s grace, but they did not want to acknowledge it. And they continued to oppose Baba and Ananda Marga just as before.

### Spiritual Cure for a Deadly Disease

Although Pranay had given strict instructions that nobody should approach Baba with any kind of mundane appeal, it was not possible to stop everyone from doing so. Sometimes even non-Margis approached the Margis with a request to place their worldly problems before Baba. Once, Virendra Kumar Asthana received an appeal from the Chief Minister of Bihar who sought Baba’s help on behalf of someone else. Asthana recalled during his interview:

One day in 1957 the personal assistant of the Chief Minister of Bihar, who was an acquaintance of mine, called me with a strange request. At that time I was posted in Patna as the assistant collector of Customs and Central Excise. The caller said that the wife of a very senior officer, Saroj Lal, had been diagnosed with cancer, and the disease was in its terminal stage. The caller said the Chief Minister had personally requested me to plead with Baba to grace the lady by curing her of the deadly disease. It was known among several high-ranking officers of the Bihar Government that Baba

had cured several deadly diseases such as tuberculosis by his mere touch or even just a wish. However, I knew that I would not be able to pass on this request to Baba, as the lady was not initiated. So I replied to the caller that since the disease was already in an advanced stage, it was too late to do anything and that I did not wish to approach Baba over this matter at such a late stage. Nevertheless, when I went to Jamalpur on my next visit, I did mention it to him. I also informed him of the reply I had given.

Baba approved of my reply. He said, “See, Virendra, I don’t want to be known as a miracle worker. I haven’t come to this world for that. I have certain things to do for society and I don’t want crowds of people coming to me with their worldly problems. That would prevent me from doing the work I have come for. Even those Margis who I cure, I do so because their faith and dependence on me compels me to do it for them. But I don’t like you all projecting me as a miracle worker. Moreover, I don’t want to oblige a person because of his high rank or because an important person has taken interest in the matter.”

I understood what Baba was saying. After a few days the person called me again with the same request, and I gave an excuse for not being able to help him.

However, when a Margi faced a similar problem, Baba dealt with it very differently. In those days many officers of the Central Excise and Customs Department had been initiated because of Customs Collector Raghuvir Prasad and several top officers including me who were active Margis.

At the end of 1958 I was transferred from Patna to Allahabad. One day a Margi officer from our department reported to me, “Sir, our Sethi is seriously ill.”

“What’s the problem?” I asked.

“It is not yet sure. From the initial tests, the doctors suspect that he has lung cancer. But there is also a remote chance that it could turn out to be tuberculosis, for which there is some chance of a cure. But if it is cancer, there is absolutely no hope.”

Om Prakash Sethi was an inspector of our department posted in Allahabad. He came from Lucknow and had taken initiation from me a few months earlier. He had been a chain smoker before becoming a Margi. Perhaps his long years of heavy smoking had finally caught up with him.

“Sir, he has gone for a final check-up in Lucknow and we will come to know the exact details only after that.”

I closed my eyes and mentally wished that it would turn out to be tuberculosis and not cancer, so that there would at least be some hope of a cure.

A couple of days later, we heard that the doctors had finally declared that Sethi was suffering from cancer. One evening he came to my house with his wife. He appeared completely devastated. He had just turned thirty-two and his wife had had a baby a few months earlier. His wife broke down in front of me and begged me to request Baba to save her husband. She said that the doctors had given Sethi only a few months to live and wanted to prepare everyone’s minds for the eventuality. As Baba had told me that he did not like people approaching him with worldly requests, I remained noncommittal. Then she approached my wife, Shrirama. Seeing her in tears, Shrirama was deeply moved. She assured Sethi’s wife that she would herself take the matter to Baba. After they left, Shrirama requested me, “You should go to Jamalpur as soon as possible and talk to Baba about it.”

“Shrirama, that is not possible. You know only too well how Baba dislikes such requests,” I replied, showing reluctance.

“How can you say that? You have to do something for Om Prakash, as he is not only your assistant but also your initiate. Don’t you see that his wife is too young to

become a widow and that only recently she has had a baby? This is not the time to hesitate.”

Shrirama persisted. Seeing me unmoved, she became upset and said that she would go with me to Jamalpur and would appeal to Baba herself. So the following Saturday we left for Jamalpur. Shrirama obtained special permission to join the evening walk with Baba, as women were generally not permitted to accompany him. In the field she informed Baba of Sethi’s condition and the doctor’s prognosis. She told him about his young wife and baby who would be orphaned if he died.

After listening to her patiently, Baba said, “What can I do about it, Shrirama? Don’t you know that everyone has to undergo the consequences of their past samskaras?”

“Baba, if you want, you can free the family from this samskara. Unless you grace them, his young wife and small baby will be orphaned. Please have compassion on them,” persisted Shrirama. Seeing Baba’s apparent reluctance, Shrirama requested him again and again.

Finally he seemed to relent. He said, “All right. Don’t worry. Ask Virendra what should be done. I authorize him to treat the patient, and whatever he does will work.”

Actually I had no idea what should be done to treat Sethi. At that time, the book *Yogic Treatments* was available only in Bengali. At first I thought of consulting the book on the treatment Baba had prescribed for cancer. On a further rethinking I also felt that Baba’s comment that he had authorized me to treat Sethi was said in jest. Whatever it was, I was certain that once Baba had said that Sethi would recover, he definitely would. So I concluded that Baba’s grace was the most potent medicine in this case and nothing else was needed.

I went back and taught Sethi Guru Dhyana and encouraged him to practice it for long hours. That was the only thing that occurred to my mind at that moment.[^1] A fortnight later the symptoms of cancer disappeared. Soon after that the doctors declared him free of the disease. It was a major sensation in our office. After his recovery Om Prakash became very active in the Marga and later became an acharya. Several of his relatives became Margis too. He sowed the seeds of the Marga in the capital city of Lucknow and became a pillar of Ananda Marga there. The following year he invited Baba to hold DMC in Lucknow. Baba stayed in Sethi’s house, and DMC was held on the roof of his house. Over the years a few more DMCs were held in the same place and Baba stayed with him on every occasion. Sometime later his niece dedicated her life to the Marga and became a *sanyasini*.

### Fulfilling a Frivolous Desire

Although Baba scrupulously kept away from the public to prevent people from flooding him with requests to fulfil their worldly desires, the Margis regularly approached him with such requests. In the early days he often indulged devoted Margis who came to him with worldly requests, some of which were quite frivolous. However, with the passage of time, Margis realized that Baba disliked it and they gradually stopped bothering him with their personal problems.

Jiyalal Gupta replaced Asthana as the assistant collector of Customs and Central Excise in Bhagalpur. On Asthana’s urging he was initiated and became a good sadhaka. In January 1958 after a short stint in Bhagalpur, Jiyalal was unexpectedly transferred to Jamnagar in

[^1]: Several years later Baba prescribed long Guru Dhyana as a treatment for cancer. He explained the science behind its effect in curing cancer. He also prescribed certain procedures to be followed before and after the practice of Guru Dhyana.

Gujarat. He did not want to leave in the middle of the academic year as it would disturb his daughter's education. In addition, he preferred to go somewhere in Punjab. The officer who was to replace him arrived, and the official handover of responsibilities was scheduled for the next morning. In the evening Jiyalal casually expressed the difficulties he would be facing because of the untimely transfer to some local acharyas who were working under him. A group of them who were posted in his office—Tapeshvar, Ananta Thakur, Mahadev and Rameshvar—discussed the matter and decided to send someone to Jamalpur immediately to request Baba to stop the transfer before the next morning. They chose Rameshvar as their emissary, but he was unwilling to go because he knew that Baba did not like Margis approaching him with worldly requests. However, due to pressure from the others, he grudgingly consented.

It was already late and Rameshvar rushed to the station to catch the late evening train to Jamalpur. During the journey, he mentally apologized to Baba again and again and expressed his inability to avoid the assigned task. Knowing that the train would arrive at Jamalpur late at night, he fervently hoped that he would be able to catch Baba before he returned home from his evening walk.

When he reached Jamalpur, it was close to 11 pm, and just as he came out of the station, he saw Baba and a few Margis coming down from the footbridge at the side of the station. Baba had introduced a rule stipulating that Margis should take prior permission from the general secretary before approaching him for anything. In obedience to this rule, Rameshvar ran past Baba and the group of Margis and raced off to Rampur Colony to meet Pranay to get permission to meet Baba. As he ran, he realized that the distance from the railway station to Rampur Colony and then to Keshavpur was nearly three times the distance that Baba would cover on his way home. Knowing how fast Baba walked, Rameshvar kept praying to him mentally to slow down and wait for him.

When he reached the Rampur Colony jagrti, he hurriedly briefed the general secretary about the purpose of his visit and requested permission to meet Baba. Pranay understood how the group of acharyas had compelled Rameshvar to bring the request for Baba's consideration against his will. So he very reluctantly gave him permission, but not before cautioning him that from then on no one should disturb Baba with such minor problems. From Rampur Colony Rameshvar ran towards Keshavpur, praying all the while that Baba would wait for him.

The road was completely deserted, and from a distance he could see Baba slowly walking towards his residence, pausing now and then to discuss something with the Margis. Just as he reached his home, Baba turned around and gestured to Rameshvar not to hurry. As Rameshvar came near to Baba he was gasping for breath.

Baba said, "Rameshvar, first relax for a while. I saw you coming when you were near the station and how, instead of talking to me, you first went to take permission from the general secretary. I appreciate your sense of discipline. And I know why you have come."

"Yes, Baba, you know that I have been compelled to do a job which I really didn't want to do," grumbled Rameshvar and then explained in detail everything that had transpired in the office.

Baba listened to him quietly and then asked, "What does Jiyalal want?"

"If he had a choice, he would prefer to be transferred after April, as that is when his only daughter will appear for her intermediate examinations. He thinks that if he is transferred now, it will disturb her preparations for the board examinations. He would prefer to be posted in Amritsar or somewhere in Punjab, as that would be closer to his hometown in Jammu."

After Rameshvar finished, Baba looked up at the sky for a few seconds and then with a deep sigh turned to him and said, "Alright, tell Jiyalal that things will happen as he wishes."

Rameshvar was visibly relaxed when he returned to the office the next morning. He briefed Jiyalal and the others about what had happened in Jamalpur and gave them Baba's

message. The news spread like wildfire among the office staff. Some made taunting remarks. A few said it would be impossible to stop the transfer at that late stage when the charge handover process had already started. The new officer came to the office and started to draft the charge handover report. After it was completed, the outgoing and incoming officers were just about to affix their signatures to the report when a call came from Patna saying that Jiyalal’s transfer had been cancelled and that he should continue his service there until further notice. The order originated from the head office in New Delhi. The entire office was stunned to hear the news. They were unable to understand how it could have happened. Both Jiyalal and his replacement were relieved, as neither of them wanted the transfer. In the month of May Jiyalal was transferred to Amritsar according to his wishes.

### Curing an Alcoholic

Pandit Surya Narayan Jha, a music teacher from Bhagalpur, had far greater need of Baba's help than Jiyalal. He was an incorrigible alcoholic. At any time of the day it would be rare to find him sober. As it was affecting his professional life, he took initiation in the Marga in the hope that through meditation he would be cured of this scourge. But he was unable to meditate because he would start his morning with a glass of alcohol and would continue drinking until he went to bed. During the DMC at Trimohan in January 1958 he sang devotional songs before Baba. Baba appreciated his voice, saying it was very sweet and melodious.

On the full moon of November 1960 a DMC was held in Dumka. Harindra, the younger brother of Aniruddha from Trimohan, persuaded Surya Narayan to attend.

As Baba was about to go for General Darshan, Harindra informed Baba about Surya Narayan's alcoholism. Baba asked him to ensure that Surya Narayan was present in the gathering. During the darshan Baba pointed out the mistakes of some of the Margis, and they were either made to promise to rectify themselves or to do *tiktiks* (knee bends while holding the ears), depending on the gravity of their mistakes. He also asked Surya Narayan to stand up.

Then he asked him, “Are you in the habit of committing any serious mistakes?”

“Yes, Baba.”

“Don’t you deserve punishment for that?”

“Yes, Baba.”

“Alright, do ten tiktiks.”

After the darshan was over, Harindra went to Baba's room and said, “Baba, just a few tiktiks will not help Surya Narayan. I want him to be completely cured of his alcoholism.”

“Harindra, don’t worry. I assure you that Surya Narayan will stop drinking.”

“But Baba he has been an alcoholic for more than twenty years and several times he has unsuccessfully tried to cure himself of this problem. He starts drinking early in the morning and it goes on until late at night. He did not want to come here because he thought he would not be able to remain without alcohol for so long, and we had to pressurise him to attend the DMC. So please do something more for him.”

Harindra wanted Baba to do something special to cure him.

“Alright, call him here.”

Harindra ran to fetch him. But Surya Narayan was nowhere to be seen. Harindra learned that after receiving punishment in the darshan, Surya Narayan had become afraid and left without telling anyone. Upon reaching home, the first thing he did was to take out a bottle of alcohol from the cabinet. He had not taken a drink since the morning and was feeling very restless. His hands were trembling from alcohol deficiency and he had a severe headache. He quickly poured himself a glass of alcohol and was about to take it when he felt a nauseating smell. He couldn’t understand why, as it had been his favorite drink for the past two decades. Despite the nauseating smell, he forced down a few gulps of the drink but immediately threw

up everything. Not wanting to give up that easily, he tried a few more times to take the alcoholic drink but every time he took it, he became terribly nauseated and had to abandon his plan. After that incident, Surya Narayanan never touched alcohol again.

### Missing Manuscript

Whenever the Margis faced any problem for which they could not find a solution, whether it was personal or organizational, they would ask Baba for help. Jogendar was an officer in the Customs and Central Excise Department and was introduced to the Marga in late 1955 by Nagina. A year later, he was trained as an acharya. He recalled how Baba helped him when he was in a particularly difficult predicament:

> Once during a visit to Jamalpur, the general secretary, Pranayda, gave me the Hindi manuscript of *Subhashita Samgraha Part 3* and asked me to supervise its printing in Patna. So I gave it to a local printer there. Once he had completed the preliminary typesetting, I was asked to proofread it. I left the manuscript on the worktable in our office in Exhibition Road, but when I went to look for it the next day, to my dismay it was nowhere to be found. For another two days I and two others searched every nook and cranny of the office in vain. It was a busy office with a lot of activity and a large number of visitors passing through every day. I realized that I should not have left such an important document in such a busy place and deeply regretted it. A second copy of the manuscript was not available and without it proofreading the manuscript was impossible. I was in a dilemma and did not know what to do. I was under great pressure and cursed myself for my lack of responsibility. Seeing no other option, I decided to go to Jamalpur the following day to seek Baba's help. As soon as Pranayda saw me, he asked when the book would be ready. As I could not tell him that the manuscript was missing, I replied, "Pranayda, it is in the process of being completed, but now I can't give you an exact date. I will tell you later."
>
> It was Sunday and Baba came for darshan around noontime. I immediately went into his room and prostrated before him. After I got up, he said with a gentle smile, "My Jogendar seems to have been a little worried for the last two or three days. What's the matter?"
>
> "Baba, you know everything. I have committed a dreadful mistake." I then fell silent, unable to muster the courage to continue.
>
> "Oh, you are talking about the *Subhashita Samgraha* Hindi manuscript?"
>
> "Yes Baba. It was a big lapse on my part and I deserve punishment for it." I felt somewhat relieved that Baba was not angry with me.
>
> "Yes, you have made a mistake. You should have been more responsible with such an important matter, but you have already suffered a lot on account of it." He paused for a while and then continued with a gentle smile, "Go and check the top left hand corner of the big rack in the inside room, and there is a chance that you will find it there in a file underneath a register."
>
> With that he turned to talk to the others. Although I felt very relieved, I still could not forgive myself. I thought that Baba should have scolded me for my carelessness. So when Baba started his discourse, I couldn't properly focus on what he was saying. I was still thinking that he should have given me some kind of punishment as atonement or at least scolded me.
>
> Such thoughts were preying upon my mind when Baba suddenly said as part of his discourse, "Human beings commit mistakes. But the biggest atonement is sincere repentance." Then he looked into my eyes and said, "Do you understand, my little boy?" and continued his talk.

His words lifted my spirits and dissipated the dark shadows of guilt that had been plaguing me. After the darshan was over, I told Pranayda that the book would be ready for delivery in a fortnight.

"What's going on? Only a couple of hours ago you said that you couldn't give a fixed date and now suddenly you are so definite?" inquired Pranayda.

"Yes, things have changed since Baba's darshan," I replied with a smile, without revealing what had happened.

As I departed from Jamalpur, I felt as if a heavy burden had been lifted from me. Indeed as Baba said, for the last few days I had been feeling tremendous stress because of the missing manuscript. The train was late, and it was close to midnight when I reached Patna. From the railway station I went straight to the Exhibition Road office. I knocked on the door and someone opened it. Everyone was surprised to see me in the office at that late hour. I said with excitement, "I got it! I know where it is!"

"What are you talking about? What did you get?" asked the office in-charge, somewhat bewildered.

"I know where the missing manuscript is."

"How do you know? And at this late hour why are you taking the trouble to look for it? You could have waited until the morning."

Without stopping to explain, I went to the next room and switched on the light. Some people were sleeping there and they woke up due to the disturbance. Apologizing to them for the inconvenience, I tried to reach the exact location on the rack that Baba had indicated, but as it was slightly beyond my reach I had to stretch to get it. Seeing that I was struggling for something, they asked many questions. But I was too excited to answer them. I stretched a bit more and pulled out a file from underneath a register, and quickly opened it. There it was, the missing manuscript, which several of us had looked for in vain for three long days! I closed my eyes in gratitude and mentally thanked Baba. A tear or two dropped from my eyes. Everyone else shared my excitement and felt relieved that the manuscript had been found.

The office in-charge asked me in a surprised tone, "Acharyaji, how did you find out where it was and that too so late in the night? Was it revealed to you in a dream?"

"No dada. I found out from the one who knows everything. I have just returned from Jamalpur."

### Divine Sentinels

One day in July 1955 Baba was travelling by car to Bhagalpur for a DMC. Along the way there was a traffic jam. Since they were in a hurry, Pranay went to investigate the matter. He discovered that the police were checking documents of all the vehicles. Pranay informed the police officer in charge of the highway patrol that the guru of Ananda Marga was in the car and requested him to check their documents forthwith and allow them to pass without having to wait in line. However he refused to oblige, curtly replying that he would not show any preference to anyone and that all the vehicles had to wait in queue. After a long and tiring wait in the summer heat, the documents of Baba's vehicle were inspected. Baba commented to Pranay that the name of the officer was Rambahadur Singh, that he was a strong moralist, and that both he and his wife were spiritually inclined. He asked Pranay to send an acharya from the Police Department to initiate him.

Soon after returning to Jamalpur, Pranay instructed Acharya Kishun Singh to contact the officer and introduce him to the Marga. A few days later Rambahadur Singh, the deputy superintendent of police, was initiated. He later became a great devotee of Baba.

After some time he was transferred to the post of deputy superintendent of highway vigilance at Barhi, an important intersection of the Grand Trunk Road and the Ranchi-Patna Highway. It was a potentially lucrative post with huge scope for taking bribes from the coal

and timber mafia, but Rambahadur was a staunch moralist. His unrelenting strictness and vigilance created many enemies for him. But these qualities and his ardent devotion endeared him to Baba. On several occasions while passing through Barhi on his way to Ranchi or on his return, Baba stopped at Rambahadur's house without prior notice. He ate whatever simple food he was offered by Rambahadur's wife, Lakshmi Devi, who was also a great devotee. They loved Baba and treated him more like a family member than as a guru, and Baba responded in a similar manner. Once in 1959, while Rambahadur was on highway patrol, he saw Baba's car approaching. Kedarnath, who was in the driver's seat, stopped the car. Rambahadur rushed to open the door and reverentially greeted Baba, touching his feet. Baba blessed him and asked lovingly, "How are you, Rambahadur?"

"By your grace I am fine, Baba."

"But you don't look so well. Have a check up with a good doctor. You should take care of your health."

"I have been working very hard and not taking proper rest. Baba, when you are my caretaker and my doctor, why should I worry? Please take some rest at my residence before continuing your journey."

"Today I am short of time, so I can't stop now. But I will surely come next time."

With this assurance Baba continued his journey towards Ranchi. Rambahadur thought that he had seen a tinge of pain in Baba's face when he inquired about his health. A few days earlier during the DMC in Hajipur Baba had cautioned him to take care of his health. Rambahadur tried to put aside any negative thoughts about his health by mentally surrendering his care to Baba. However, a few days after Baba's second warning, he fell severely ill. He consulted several doctors, but they were unable to diagnose his problem. After several heavy doses of wrong medicine, he was finally found to be suffering from typhoid. Despite being late, proper treatment was started, and Rambahadur soon recovered. But just when he was finally cured of the typhoid, he came down with other ailments. He developed many complications - lack of appetite, indigestion and constant diarrhea. A few days later his left eye started swelling, causing him severe pain. He consulted an ophthalmologist. But his condition only worsened, and the pain increased. As his eye deteriorated further, he decided to go to Patna to consult a specialist.

One morning towards the end of August 1959 Rambahadur left for Patna in a hired car before dawn, accompanied by a cousin. His official residence was in an isolated place in Barhi, and this was a cause of great concern to his wife, Lakshmi. In addition to creating many enemies amongst the local coal and timber mafia because of his non-compromising honesty, there were also threats to the family's security from his junior police colleagues who had been deprived of their corrupt earnings and who were angered by his strict adherence to morality. On top of that, Barhi and its surrounding areas were plagued with criminals. Rambahadur's trusted assistant was on long leave. Since Rambahadur would be away for a few days and Lakshmi would be alone with the children and an elderly helper, she felt apprehensive about their security. Before leaving for Patna, Rambahadur comforted his worried wife, "We have enemies because we have been living according to the dictates of Dharma. Baba will surely be there to protect you and the children. I am leaving you all in his divine care. So don't worry."

Lakshmi lay awake until dawn, sick with anxiety. Gripped by fear, she meditated on Baba seeking his protection. When she came out of the house after sunrise, she saw two ferocious looking black dogs, much bigger than normal ones, sitting at the entrance to the house. She had never seen them before. At first she was afraid to go near them, but soon discovered that they were very friendly towards her and the children. Later one of them took up a position near the entrance of the house, while the other walked around the back as if on patrol duty. These mysterious guards were a source of great solace to Lakshmi. Whatever food she cooked, she shared it with the strange canine sentinels. With strangers they behaved

like ferocious guard dogs, growling and barking, and never allowed anyone to enter the compound without Lakshmi’s permission.

In Patna Rambahadur’s treatment by a specialist ophthalmologist of the Patna Medical College Hospital failed to yield any result. On the contrary, his condition deteriorated even further. The doctor said that the wrong medicine he had taken earlier for the treatment of his typhoid had caused the problem with his eye. Soon he started to lose the vision in his left eye. The specialist’s prognosis did not bode well for Rambahadur. The doctor said that he would never get the vision back in his left eye and warned him about the possibility of his right eye becoming affected as well. Rambahadur stayed in the hospital for more than a month. In the meanwhile one of the eye muscles ruptured, causing his eye to bleed and the pain to increase. He consulted more specialists but all to no avail. The unbearable pain and the prospect of going completely blind distressed Rambahadur tremendously. In addition, the money that he had brought with him was almost exhausted, and the continued stay in Patna for the treatment was becoming a great financial burden. Completely frustrated, he lost his will to live and prayed to Baba to take him from this world. His cousin and the Margis who visited him chided him for losing hope, saying that he had a wife and three small children depending on him and that he should not give up so easily and have faith in Baba. Some Margis suggested that he should write a letter to Baba about his condition. Rambahadur initially hesitated, as he did not want to bother Baba by asking him for any favors. However, the Margis argued that if he could pray to Baba to take away his life, why he couldn’t write to Baba about the condition of his health. Due to the Margis’ constant urging, he finally wrote a letter to Baba describing his condition.

The following Sunday, as soon as Baba arrived at the jagrti, he asked Pranay if there was any news from Rambahadur. Pranay informed him that a Margi had come from Patna that morning with a letter from him. After the letter was read to him, Baba dictated a reply to Pranay, asking Rambahadur not to worry and telling him to constantly chant his *Ishta mantra*. If he could not chant it sitting down, he should do it lying in bed. Baba instructed Pranay to immediately send the letter through the same messenger.

Rambahadur was elated to receive the message of assurance from Baba and started to chant his mantra as directed. Soon the pain and swelling began to subside, and his condition improved greatly. It was *Dussehra*, an important Hindu festival, and he was restless to be with his family during the festival. Ignoring the doctor’s advice to stay in hospital for a few more days, he decided to go home before the pain had completely healed. He arrived late at night on the 8th of October after an absence of about forty days, anxious to know how his wife and children had coped during his long absence.

After he refreshed himself, Lakshmi explained how the two mysterious dogs had been guarding them ever since he left, and that she had never felt insecure with such ferocious protectors around. Rambahadur’s eyes filled with tears as his wife recounted her strange experience. He was sure that these canine guards had been sent by Baba to protect his family in his absence. Accompanied by Lakshmi, he went out to look for them. However, the dogs were nowhere to be seen. They appeared to have vanished into thin air.

Rambahadur said, “When I left for Patna, I entrusted your safety and the children’s safety to Baba. See how he took care of all of you. These dogs came mysteriously when you needed them, and now that their task is over, they have disappeared just as mysteriously.”

Rambahadur told her all that had transpired in Patna and how Baba had sent him a message of hope when he had become completely dejected about his life.

Finally he said, “Just as he took care of you and relieved me of most of the pain and swelling in my eye, he will solve the rest of the problem and restore my vision as well.”

One day at noon, towards the end of October, Lakshmi was pleasantly surprised by Baba’s sudden arrival, accompanied by two acharyas, Devichand Sharma and Balendu Bushan Sinha, the deputy director of mining. He was on his way to Ranchi in Balendu’s car

and said that he wanted to take a bath, meditate and leave after lunch. He was in a hurry and instructed Lakshmi not to make anything special but to quickly cook some simple food. Rambahadur rushed home from his office as soon as he heard about Baba's arrival. The atmosphere in the house that had become gloomy after his illness suddenly brightened up with Baba's unexpected arrival.

As Baba ate, Rambahadur took the opportunity to ask him about the mysterious dogs. Baba smiled and said, "They were divine sentinels sent to protect your family due to the grave security threat they faced. *Dharma rakshati rakshitah.* Those who protect Dharma will be protected by Dharma."

After lunch, as Baba was preparing to leave, Rambahadur and his wife prostrated before him. "Are you not coming with me, Rambahadur?" asked Baba.

The unexpected invitation surprised Rambahadur. "Yes, Baba, I am," he replied without a second thought.

Baba told him, "Rambahadur, you are on duty now. So write an application for leave." Rambahadur hastily wrote an application and asked his assistant to leave it on the office table while Lakshmi quickly packed his luggage.

Baba stayed in Ranchi for two days. On the third day he left for Jamalpur in Amulyaratan's car by a different route, accompanied by Rambahadur and Devichand.

As the sun was about to set, Baba said, "Rambahadur, Amulya has been driving non-stop for about six hours. Why don't you take over the wheel?"

The suggestion took everyone by surprise. Rambahadur thought, "How can I risk driving with vision in only one eye on a bumpy road full of potholes and that too when Baba is in the car?"

Almost immediately, as if in reply, he heard a voice from within telling him, "Why do you have to worry? The force that guides the stars guides you too."

The roads were badly damaged due to unusually heavy rains that year, and that considerably slowed down their speed. Soon it became dark, but Rambahadur somehow managed to steer clear of the potholes and drive safely. There was no indication at all that he was blind in one eye and losing vision in the other. As it was dark and they were still more than two hours away from Jamalpur, Amulyaratan proposed to halt at a government guesthouse along the way and continue their journey the next morning. Baba hesitantly agreed. The next morning Rambahadur found that the eye pain had recurred and that he was again blind in his left eye.

After this everyone felt that Baba alone could cure Rambahadur since the doctors had failed to cure him. They spent three more days in Jamalpur enjoying Baba's divine company. Both Devichand and Amulyaratan wanted to request him to grace Rambahadur and save him from the possibility of going blind. However, they didn't get a suitable opportunity to talk to him about it. On the last day of their stay all three of them were present with Baba during the evening walk, after which they accompanied him back to his residence.

Before parting company, Baba said, "Amulya, drop Rambahadur at his house on your way back."

Seeing this as their last chance, Devichand pleaded, "Baba, the doctors have all given up on Rambahadur. Now, without your grace, nothing will prevent him from going blind."

Baba replied with seeming indifference, "Rambahadur is suffering from the samskaras of his past life. Don't you know that in the Tantras it has been said about samskaras:

"The samskaras of one's past actions be they good or bad, do not end even after billions of ages, unless they are undergone through the experience of pain or pleasure. This is the unalterable law of creation."

He then paused for a while. Everyone thought it meant that he was not going to grace Rambahadur. Then he suddenly said in a most affectionate tone, "But when I see the suffering

of those who follow Dharma and strictly adhere to the principles of morality and spirituality, I make some exceptions to the law of Nature."

Then Baba called Rambahadur to come closer and pressed his left eye with his right thumb, and then placed his palm over both his eyes.

After that he said, "Go Rambahadur. Your eyes will not bother you anymore." Rambahadur touched Baba's feet and, deeply moved by Baba's boundless grace, began to weep.

After Baba went inside his house, Devichand and Amulyaratan asked Rambahadur what he had felt. He replied excitedly, "I am able to see with my left eye even in the dim moonlight. I can't be sure whether my eyesight is completely normal or not, till I try to read a book in normal light. In any case, I am so happy with what Baba has done."

As soon as they reached the jagrti, Rambahadur picked up a newspaper and read it first with one eye and then with the other in order to test his vision. "My sight has been completely restored. I am fully cured. Baba has saved me from going blind." He repeated this over and over again in great excitement.

CHAPTER 28

# Divine Intoxication

From the early years of Ananda Marga quite a few of the disciples had peculiar spiritual experiences. During *dharmachakra* it was common for people to exhibit occult symptoms such as weeping, shouting or laughing, particularly during the initial stages of their sadhana. In Baba's presence, such symptoms were more common and were intensified. In the book *A Guide to Human Conduct* Baba explained that these symptoms were caused by the effect of subtle mental vibrations on the various glands of the body. Such behavior sometimes scared away new initiates or created misunderstanding in the mind of the public. At times it led to even more serious problems.

Acharya Sukhen of Krishnanagar was a participant in one such episode that took several twists and turns:

"Although I had seen several people display this type of abnormal behavior after starting to practice sadhana, I saw the most interesting example of occult symptoms in one of my initiates, Bijoy Kumar Rai, a junior advocate. He was initiated in the beginning of 1957. After practicing meditation for a few weeks, he started manifesting several unusual behaviors. Whenever he shut himself in a room to do meditation, he would start to sing and dance. People from the locality would gather at his house to watch his strange behavior. Soon his whole lifestyle also underwent a radical change. His wife and mother grew very worried about what was happening to him and accused us of teaching him a technique of meditation which had made him insane.

Usually at night he would sit for long meditation. It was then that he was most likely to start dancing and singing. One night at around two o'clock there was a knock at my door. A local Margi was standing there panting. He said, "Sukhenda, Bijoy has gone mad. The public have gathered at his house, and there is a big commotion going on."

I raced over immediately and found that a small crowd had gathered around Bijoy, who was sitting in lotus posture with his hands together and eyes closed as if in meditation.

He was muttering, "Do you think that I am pretending all these things? Seeing me, do you feel that I am faking it all? You won't understand until you have the same experiences that I am having."

It was clear that he was saying all this to his wife and mother. I shook him and ordered him to open his eyes. In a rebuking tone, I asked, "Bijoy, what is all this madness? All these people have gathered here due to your eccentric behavior."

Bijoy opened his eyes and stared at me as if he had just awoken from a stupor. "Sukhenda, why have you come so late at night? And why have all these people gathered here?"

"You did not leave me with any other choice. You have been behaving like a madman and gathered them all here."

First, I remonstrated with Bijoy and then explained to him what he had been doing.

In a surprised tone, he asked, "Is it all true, Sukhenda? Have I really been doing such things?"

I then dispersed the crowd, saying that Bijoy was normal and that there was nothing wrong with him. Later, I explained to the family members that these were symptoms of sadhana and that they should not be worried. The next night, there was

again a knock at my door. The same Margi was again urging me to rush to Bijoy’s house. I hurried over and with some effort normalised Bijoy.

The same thing was repeated for the next four or five days. The problem grew more complicated because Bijoy’s family members thought he was going insane and started to treat him accordingly. As a result the general public turned against Ananda Marga. They accused us of practicing black magic and threatened us with severe consequences. Such misconceptions hindered our Marga work. We became exasperated due to the problems Bijoy and his family were creating. The public’s reactions added to our problems. I was at a complete loss and didn’t know how to handle the situation.

One morning I received an unexpected letter from the general secretary, Pranayda. It said, “Baba has said that what has happened to Bijoy is a good thing. It has been caused by a slight upward movement of his kundalini. His strange behavior is not due to madness. There is no need to worry about the threats you are receiving from the public. Anyone trying to disturb you will be blown away like chaff in the wind. No one will be able to do you any harm. Keep doing your Marga work. In the meantime, make sure that Bijoy goes to court every day. Gradually he will become normal again.”

I tried to follow Baba’s instructions, but Bijoy’s family did not permit me to take him to the court. They confined him in one room and consulted a Muslim fakir, who gave them a medicinal herb, which, he assured them, would cure Bijoy. However, instead of curing him, it caused him severe stomach problem, and his physical condition deteriorated. Whenever we went to visit him, his family and the local people abused us. We asked the family to allow us to take care of Bijoy, assuring them that he would become completely normal under our supervision. They refused. We said that in that case we were relinquishing all responsibility for him and the family would have to take sole responsibility for whatever happened to him.

To find out what really had happened Bijoy Kumar Rai was interviewed. He vividly described what happened to him after his initiation:

I was a devotee of Krishna before I was initiated by Acharya Sukhen Naik. My attraction for Lord Krishna was different from the feelings of other people towards Him. For me Krishna was a living god and I used to feel that He resided inside me. However I longed for a deeper experience of Krishna.

Thinking that meditation would provide this experience, I took initiation and practiced it. After a few months of sincere effort, I suddenly started to have strange spiritual experiences. I would smell a sweet aroma all around me. I did not know where it came from. It gave me a feeling of spiritual intoxication. I was floating in bliss and all I wanted was to remain in that state of divine ecstasy forever. This experience completely changed my outlook and I started to see the world in an entirely different light. Everything appeared to be an expression of Divine Effulgence. Because of that, I was not able to do my work in a normal manner.

I usually did all the shopping for my family. I went to the market to buy vegetables, but I felt that they were all full of life. So I could not buy them. I went to buy fish, but felt that the fish were also part of me.

“What has been part of me has been killed,” I thought. “How can I eat something which has been part of me and has been killed?”

I felt the pain of the dead fish and I cried continuously, thinking about the suffering they had undergone. Gradually I started to have the realization that everything was a part of me and I was a part of everything. It is a state of mind that people can’t understand unless they themselves attain it. I related to people and things around me through the prism of that lofty state of mind. Whenever I had money, if anyone needed it, I would ask them to take whatever they wanted from my pocket because what was

mine was theirs too. There was no difference between other people and me. When I was in need of money, I felt that the money of others was mine as well. But people did not share it with me. I saw that people felt ‘this is mine and that is yours.’ Sometimes I wondered if something was wrong with my new-found realization. My desire for food diminished, as I felt inexhaustible energy inside me. At times I felt that there was nothing I couldn't do. Once I wanted to test whether the energy inside me was stronger than electricity. I caught hold of a live wire, and to my great surprise, I did not get any electric shock. A tremendous transformation was taking place within me. Externally my body was very hot, and I felt physically very uneasy, but internally I was very blissful.

I constantly repeated my mantra and wasn’t able to take even a single breath without repeating it at the same time. The mantra continued even during my sleep. I began to see divinity everywhere and in everything. Due to this sudden change in my mindset and the surges of ecstasy I experienced, I was unable to maintain balance in my worldly life. As a lawyer, I had to go to court. But everything in the court appeared unreal to me. For me the only reality was that I was an inextricable part of the Supreme Entity and everybody else was also a part of it. So why were all these unnecessary quarrelling and why these feuds? I felt it was all meaningless.”

Bijoy was the only breadwinner in his family. His relatives became very worried seeing the sudden change in him. His condition affected them financially too, because he stopped going to court regularly and that caused his income to dwindle. They took him to a renowned psychiatrist in Calcutta. The doctor wanted to hear from Bijoy himself what his problem was.

Bijoy said, “Doctor Sahib, I am perfectly alright. Nearly a year ago, I started to perform sadhana. I am in a constant state of bliss due to the meditation. It has given me a new perspective on life. My outlook on the objective world is very different now. I see everything as a divine expression. The only problem I have is that my family members are unable to understand this change in me in the right perspective. They are convinced that I have become insane, and they are taking me to one place after another for treatment.”

After a thorough examination, the doctor declared that Bijoy was not insane and advised the family to take him to the people who had taught him meditation, as they alone would be able to cure him of whatever abnormality he had developed. However, instead of following the doctor’s advice, they filed a case against Ananda Marga. The whole town was talking about Bijoy, saying that the Ananda Margis have made him insane. Some accused the Margis of being untrained yoga teachers who have spoiled the life of a simple Brahmin family. Others said that they were black magicians. Some even threatened to assault the Margis. But the Margis remained unaffected by all this because of Baba’s assurance that anyone trying to harm them would be blown away like chaff.

In the court case Bijoy’s family accused the Margis of stealing his soul. Haraprasad replied by urging the judge to order the psychiatric treatment of those who had declared a sane person insane, and made such ridiculous accusations against them. The case was finally dismissed.

A month later, they received news that Baba was planning to hold DMC in March 1958, in Amra, the native village of Nityananda in Birbhum District. Sukhen somehow convinced Bijoy’s family members to let him go with them, assuring them that Bijoy would come back completely cured.

Baba arrived by train at Labhpur station en route to Amra on the morning of 4ᵗʰ March. From there the rest of the journey was to be by bus. The Margis boarded the bus when it arrived. However, Baba continued to wait outside. As it was getting late, the bus driver requested all the remaining passengers to get on the bus quickly. Pranay then requested Baba to take his seat. Baba complied, though rather reluctantly. Strangely, when the driver tried to

start the bus, he was unable to do so despite several attempts. From what was going on, the Margis understood that Baba was waiting for someone.

After a few minutes, Baba exclaimed, "Oh, Nandu has come!"

The Margis could not see anyone. However, a short while later Sachinandan came running, jumped on the bus and apologized for being late. As soon as he got on, the engine mysteriously came to life. The Margis felt that the bus had not started because Baba was waiting for Sachinandan. They alighted at a spot where a bullock cart was waiting to take Baba across the Mayurakshi River to Amra.

Baba arrived there at around ten in the morning. Acharya Amulyaratan Sarangi was one of several people who accompanied him on this trip. About a month before, Pranay had sent him a manuscript to translate into Bengali. It was a copy of the Renaissance Universal speech that Baba had delivered in Trimohan. Soon after his arrival, Baba called Amulyaratan and inquired about the translation of the speech, as he wanted the Bengali version to be read out to the Margis that evening. Amulyaratan felt embarrassed that he had failed to carry out this important task and immediately set to work. The manuscript was four or five pages long. He found it difficult to translate the line, "All the property of this earth, movable as well as immovable, does not belong to any particular individual; rather everything is the common patrimony of all of us. Brahma, the universal father and the creator of the entire universe, is the actual owner of everything." Despite repeated efforts, Amulyaratan was not able to think of a Bengali equivalent for 'movable' and 'immovable'.

He went to Baba and reported, "Baba, I am facing a problem to find the exact Bengali translation of some English words."

Without even asking what those words were, Baba remarked, "You are a law graduate. You must have read the Transfer of Property Act."

Suddenly Amulyaratan remembered. "Yes, Baba, I remember now. It is 'Sthavar and Asthavar'," he said, recollecting the words from his law book.

Baba said, "Although that would be the appropriate translation, the people of the village are not acquainted with these words, and so while reading the translation before the village Margis, it will be better to use '*Chal*' and '*Achal*', which even ordinary village folk will understand."

When Sukhen and the other Margis from Krishnanagar reached Amra, Bijoy's condition was uppermost in their minds. Soon after Baba's arrival, they were ushered into his room. As they got up after prostrating, Baba asked, "Sukhen, how is everything in Krishnanagar?"

"Everything is fine there, Baba," replied Sukhen, hesitating to disturb Baba with Bijoy's issue in the very first meeting.

Baba then turned to the general secretary and asked with a gentle smile, "Pranay, did we not receive news recently about how a certain Margi of Muzaffarpur started to sing and dance after starting the practice of meditation and how that was helping the *prachar* work there?" Pranay nodded his head in assent. "Wasn't there similar news from Darbhanga as well? Some initially thought the Margi was mad, but soon everyone understood that his seemingly abnormal behavior was caused by his spiritually elevated state."

Pranay nodded again.

Since Baba had himself brought up the topic, Sukhen took the cue and said, "Baba, but in Krishnanagar the situation is just the other way around; we are going mad due to Bijoy."

Smiling enigmatically Baba asked, "What's the matter? What happened to you all?"

Sukhen then gave a detailed report of the situation in Krishnanagar. After listening to the whole story, Baba repeated the instructions he had asked Pranay to send by letter a few months before.

"There is nothing to worry about. What has happened to Bijoy is due to the rise of his kundalini. That has caused a sudden change in his outlook and he is finding it difficult to have a balance between the subjective reality and the objective world. That makes him behave in a

way which appears abnormal to others. Just follow my instructions and take him to the court every day. That will enable him to find the balance between the two worlds and he will become normal in a matter of days."

As Baba had not yet taken his bath or performed his other morning duties, the Margis left the room.

Later that day Haraprasad, Partha, Mantu, and some other Margis from Krishnanagar pleaded with Baba to cure Bijoy, saying that otherwise they would not be able to work in peace in Krishnanagar. Hearing this, Baba asked Haraprasad to call Bijoy. Haraprasad went looking for him and saw him sitting under a tree some distance away with his eyes closed. Haraprasad said, "Bijoy, Baba is calling you."

"Baba is everywhere. I see him in everything. So why should I go to his room?" replied Bijoy with complete indifference. When Haraprasad reported Bijoy's reply to Baba, Baba sent Partha. He too came back with the same reply. Baba then sent several other Margis from Krishnanagar, one after another, and all of them received a similar response. Some of them tried to drag Bijoy with them but were astonished at his strength; they could not budge him even an inch however hard they tried. Baba then sent Devichand Sharma who was very strong and well built. He was also unable to force Bijoy to come. All the while, young Mantu was wondering why Baba did not ask him to bring Bijoy. He was sure that he would succeed, as he had a strong influence on Bijoy.

Finally, Baba said to him, "Mantu, you should not think that I did not ask you, so go and try to bring him."

Mantu was also unable to persuade Bijoy to come and returned alone. "Alright, leave Bijoy to himself," said Baba. "He will come here very soon of his own accord."

After a short while, Bijoy appeared at the door of Baba's room.

Bijoy described during his interview how he had felt that day:

> When Baba sent several people to fetch me, I was sitting under a tree doing meditation. At that time I was in a spiritually intoxicated state. I was seeing Baba everywhere and in everything around me and was feeling an irresistible attraction to everything. I felt that it was Baba who was attracting me through all these things. Intense waves of bliss were inundating my being, and I did not want to be disturbed. So I thought that as I was feeling attracted to Baba through everything around me, why should I have to go anywhere to see him? That's why I declined to go. A little while later something happened. I felt that an irresistible attraction was pulling me to the room where Baba was staying, and soon afterwards I found myself standing before him.

Baba asked me, "How do you feel, Bijoy?"

"Baba, you know everything. Why are you asking me?"

Baba asked me to sit beside him. He then explained what was happening to me and several things related to that. But I didn't pay attention to any of it. Finally he asked me to sit near his bed and meditate. I don't know what happened to me after that.

While sitting beside Baba, Bijoy went into a spiritual trance. Baba then commented, "People think that something is wrong with Bijoy. But he is in a spiritual state caused by the sudden rise of his kundalini. This state is known as *mahabhava* and is a very high state of divine experience. If even a small part of the spiritual power that is in Bijoy were now transferred to you all, none of you would be able to tolerate it."

Baba then directed the Margis to sit in meditation.

"Those who have learned the *dhyana* lesson should do it now, and the rest of you should do *Ishvara Pranidhana*."

Haraprasad had learned Vishesh Yoga, so Baba asked him to do dhyana according to Vishesh Yoga. Soon the fragrance that usually permeated Baba's room became intense and everyone felt spiritually intoxicated. As they meditated, Baba said that he was withdrawing

the spiritual power from Bijoy and releasing it amongst all of them. Suddenly, everyone in the room felt a strong jolt, as if they had been struck by a powerful spiritual current. Sukhen vividly recalled the experience he had at that time:

A short while before, Nityananda had requested me to initiate some people in a nearby village. I had just taught meditation to one of them and was explaining how to sit and ideate before starting meditation, when suddenly I felt as if I was being lifted high above the earth by a powerful force and then thrown down again. I felt as if I was falling through infinite space and was unable to keep my balance. I thought that I had suddenly fallen ill. Somehow I managed to complete the important part of the initiation by whispering the mantra in the ear of the initiate, but after that I was unable to speak even a single word. I terminated the initiation process halfway and staggered out of the room with unsteady steps. Along the way I met Nityananda and asked him for a glass of water, saying that I was feeling unwell. As I drank, I said, "Nitai, I think I have fallen ill. While I was giving initiation, I felt as if I was being lifted up to the sky and then thrown down again. It seemed as if I was falling through endless space."

On hearing these words, Nityananda laughed and said that he had also had a similar experience. He then elaborated, "On the insistence of the Margis from Krishnanagar, Baba called Bijoy. He said that he was withdrawing all the spiritual energy from Bijoy and distributing it amongst the other Margis. Immediately, many people started to have different kinds of spiritual experiences, including me. I am sure that what you felt was also due to this."

Together they went to Baba's residence. Outside Baba's room, they saw a very unusual sight. Haraprasad was sitting in a corner, muttering, "My whole body is burning, but how blissful it is. I can't bear it. Bijoy, did you also experience something like this?"

Then Haraprasad started to roll on the ground. The other Margis from Krishnanagar were also there. They were all in a state of ecstasy. Bijoy was sitting alone in a corner. Strangely, he was the only one from Krishnanagar who looked normal, and it appeared as if he had been 'cured' of his abnormality. It took several hours for the Margis, apart from Haraprasad, to come out of their ecstatic state. Haraprasad, however, remained in ecstasy, and continued rolling on the ground for a long time. Finally he sat up still absorbed in bliss. He remained silent the entire time, with tears streaming from his closed eyes, only occasionally breaking his silence to mumble something about feeling indescribable bliss. He did not talk to anyone or take any food the whole day.

In the afternoon, Baba called some senior Margis and asked them to hold a *kabigan*, which he said was an ideal method of spreading subtle philosophical ideas among the common people in the rural areas of Bengal. Kabigan is a type of Bengali drama or debate, where opposing views are expressed through folk songs. Baba explained to them how to spread the Ananda Marga ideology through such cultural performances. He described how one group would sing about the Marga ideology and dictated a few songs as examples. Then he also suggested songs for the opposing group, who represented the traditional beliefs, and asked them to compose more songs along similar lines.

There was a public announcement in the village about the kabigan. After dinner hundreds of villagers gathered when they heard the beating of drums in the open ground nearby. The performers were in two groups—one representing the Ananda Marga ideology and the other extolling the virtues of traditional ritualistic practices. They then started a debate through melodious songs which expressed the virtue and rational nature of their beliefs. It went on until well past midnight. By the time it was over, the general public had a better perception of the salient features of the Ananda Marga ideology and the defects of their traditional rituals.

When the Margis returned from the kabigan, they saw Haraprasad still lying on the ground in a state of ecstasy, his face glowing. Pran頂いたinform informed them that Haraprasad was in savikalpa samadhi, and that Baba had indicated that he would soon return to normal

consciousness. A short time later he emerged from that blissful state and started repeating, "I am Anandamurti. I am Baba Anandamurti. How blissful it is! How blissful it is!"

When everyone retired to sleep late that night Haraprasad was still in a spiritually intoxicated state. The next morning he looked fresh and showed no signs of having spent a whole day without food or a night without sleep. What happened next was a great surprise to everyone. Haraprasad started to exhibit occult powers. He was able to read people's minds, say what they were thinking, know whether they were doing their meditation properly or not, and even say what they were thinking about during their meditation. He had also developed the capacity to see everyone's past, present, and future, and by his mere touch could put them in a spiritual trance. People flocked to him, asking him to predict their future. Interestingly, even the dogs, goats, and cattle were attracted to him and followed him wherever he went.

As he walked through the village followed by crowds of people and animals, Haraprasad looked like a spiritually intoxicated Pied Piper. He was also able to communicate with the animals and when he gave orders to the village dogs, they obeyed. As the motley group sauntered along the village lanes, an angry bull broke loose and chased some of the villagers. They shouted at the Margis to run away. However, instead of running away, Haraprasad raised his hand before the bull, and, to the great astonishment of the onlookers, it became completely docile. Haraprasad stroked it gently and then tied it to a tree. Turning to the villagers, he said, "The animals of this village are complaining that after taking a lifetime of service from them, as a reward for their loyalty, their owners sell them to the Muslim butchers to be slaughtered. Be warned that anyone who does such things will be reborn as a cow or bull or some other animal in his next life and face the same fate."

Sakaldev, the lawyer from Muzaffarpur, was buying betel leaf from a roadside stall. Haraprasad walked over to the stall and asked the stall owner, "Why are you selling betel leaf to the Margis when you know that they are not allowed to eat it?"

He then struck the man on the forehead, and he fell into a deep ditch nearby. The people thought that he was either dead or seriously injured, but when they dragged him out of the pit, they found that he was in a spiritual trance and totally unharmed. To everyone Haraprasad met, he said, "I am Anandamurti. I am Baba." Everyone he touched went into a trance. They would either fall over and roll on the ground, dance and sing, or sit quietly with a stream of tears pouring from their closed eyes, a sign that they were experiencing great inner bliss.

Rakhahari Chattopadhyay was a new Margi and a leading lawyer from Bankura. He was not at all impressed with all these strange happenings. In his eyes it all bordered on lunacy. He consciously tried to keep away from Haraprasad. Several Margis were singing and dancing in the room where he was resting, and it offended his feeling of propriety to see people publicly singing and dancing with such abandon. During lunch he was sitting in a row of people on the floor. Haraprasad approached him saying, "I am Anandamurti," and touched his forehead. Immediately the proud lawyer shed his overbearing attitude and started to sing and dance in ecstasy in front of everyone.

That day was Dol Purnima (Holi), the color festival, which was celebrated across India to welcome the arrival of spring. Baba asked Nityananda to arrange a collective meal for all the villagers. In those days, it was unthinkable for members of the higher castes to eat alongside people from the lower castes, who they considered to be untouchable. The rich would also hesitate to eat together with the poor. But the mood in Amra that day was such that the caste and class barriers broke down completely. A few orthodox, senior members of landlord families had strictly instructed their relatives not to participate in the collective meal. They decreed that anyone violating their order would be expelled from the family. Partly due to the progressive ideas generated by the kabigan the previous night and partly because people wanted to be part of the flow that Baba's presence in the village had created, all the villagers from all castes and classes, barring a few old people, cast aside their complexes and took part in the feast. The Margis also found it almost unbelievable to see people from the higher castes

eating sitting next to Harijans. Even young girls from conservative families secretly arrived to join the collective meal. That day the villagers of Amra took a very progressive step that had been unthinkable even two days earlier. As a token of his appreciation of this revolutionary action, Baba went around while everyone was taking their food, asking them if they liked it and if they would like more. This touched the hearts of the simple villagers, many of whom were seeing Baba for the first time.

Later, many of them commented how surprised they were, and wondered how they had mustered the courage to break the shackles of traditions that had been in place for centuries. Although it was a small step, it was a highly significant and revolutionary one for a conservative village like Amra. That day Baba took part in a special Ananda Marga flag-raising ceremony in honor of the important event of breaking down caste and class barriers in a remote village of Bengal. Baba said that it might appear to be a small step, but for the suppressed sections of society, it was a big leap.

Earlier, after the noon darshan, the Margis offered *avir* (colored powder) at Baba's feet, symbolizing the offering of their mental colors at the holy feet of the guru. Then they celebrated the color festival by playing with colored powders, with the young offering the colored powder at the feet of their elders in accordance with the system Baba had prescribed in *Caryacarya*. It was the first time that the Margis observed this festival with all the pomp and color of the Marga system.

The DMC was held in an enclosed pandal in front of Nityananda's house. Loudspeakers were set up outside to enable the public to listen to Baba's discourse. In the DMC that evening, Baba summed up the ecstatic feeling that many of them had experienced since the day before in the following words:

> "To proceed towards Parama Purusha one will have to jump into and drift in the vast cosmic flow. In the course of this movement, one will realize His divine sweetness. By relinquishing the feeling of being the doer of the action, one will gradually merge into the stance of the Macrocosmic Entity; one's individual flow will merge into the divine flow of the Supreme. To merge one's individual life and mind in the cosmic flow and enjoy divine sweetness is not something unnatural. Rather, to dance, laugh, and weep with such intensity that one will be branded as a lunatic is really quite natural."

At the end of his DMC discourse, Baba's final remarks were a fitting conclusion to the unusual events of the previous two days in Amra. He exhorted all to merge their individual flow in the divine flow of the Supreme Consciousness like Mahaprabhu Chaitanya had done, "causing people to madly run after him, dancing, crying, singing, and laughing in ecstatic joy. This divine flow was also expressed through Shri Krishna's flute, which resonated with such divine sweetness that people ran towards it madly, forgetting their family, culture, prestige, lineage, and so on. The *gopis* of Vrindavan left their homes and also danced, sang, and burst into laughter, intoxicated by the sound of the flute.

"In Ananda Marga, this divine flow of the Supreme Consciousness is embedded in the different lessons of spiritual meditation. Thus, those who practice it, whether in the present or the future, whether within time or beyond time, will certainly cry, sing, and dance in ecstasy, as they advance steadily towards the blissful Macrocosmic Stance."

The next morning Baba left for Jamalpur. A large crowd of villagers came to see him off. The scene was highly charged with emotion. Many were in tears. Baba's visit to Amra had created a huge stir in the hearts of the simple village folk. As Baba was about to get onto the bullock cart that was to take him across the Mayurakshi River, he saw people weeping and shouting, "Baba don't leave us, Baba don't leave us." He stopped for a while and greeted them with a very sweet smile and namaskar. His presence radiated blissful waves. As a parting message he sang a touching verse from Rabindranath Tagore:

> *Mor nam ei bale khyata hok*
> *Ami tomaderi lok,*
> *Er cheye beshi kichu nay,*
> *Ei hok shes parichaya.*
>
> [Let me be known for only one thing,
> That I belong to you all;
> Nothing more than this,
> Let this be my final identity.]

Many of the villagers accompanied Baba up to Ahamadpur station, where he caught the train to Jamalpur. Some of them were also interested to see Haraprasad, as they had heard stories about his miraculous powers. After Baba departed, the Krishnanagar Margis were waiting for their train when Haraprasad saw an old man queuing to buy a ticket. He told him that it would be better for him to go back home and spend his time with his family members instead of travelling. He then told Sukhen and the others that this man was from a well-known family in a nearby village and that he was going to die within a few hours. So it was better for him to spend his remaining hours with his family, rather than to die alone and uncared for in a distant place. The local Margis who knew the man told him that Haraprasad was a mahatma and that he had advised him to go home immediately. They didn't tell him that his end was near. The next day they heard that the man died a few hours later, as Haraprasad had foretold.

After a few stations a couple of mendicants entered the train compartment where the Krishnanagar Margis were sitting and began singing the Hare Krishna kirtan. Sukhen and Mantu offered their seats beside Haraprasad to the mendicants. Within a few minutes, they started trembling and crying. They left their seats and sat on the floor in front of Haraprasad with folded hands, and started to massage his feet. Despite his protests, they continued massaging him and pleaded with him to save them. Haraprasad repeatedly requested them to take their seats. They replied that they would not be able to sit alongside such a great soul and repeatedly requested him to bless them. For the public it was a very strange sight to see mendicants holding the feet of a family person; to the Margis it was an embarrassment. Finally, Haraprasad told them that if they wanted to be blessed, they should learn meditation and asked them to contact Sukhen. It was obvious that they had become spiritually vibrated through contact with Haraprasad, like many others in Amra village the day before.

Haraprasad's parapsychological abilities did not diminish even after they returned to Krishnanagar. His power to tell the past and future attracted many people. He even talked about people's past lives.

One day he went to the court with Sukhen. Seeing the court accountant smoking a *bidi*, Haraprasad remarked, "What a twist of fate! What a pathetic situation you are in! There was a time when you sat in a royal enclosure and smoked from an expensive hookah, while here you can't even afford a cigarette. You are puffing an ordinary bidi. This is the play of samskara."

The accountant stared at him, unable to understand what he was saying. Haraprasad continued, "In an earlier life you were Maharaja Sirish Nandi, the ruler of Murshidabad."

The accountant thought that Haraprasad was a madman who was babbling nonsense.

The abnormal behavior of Bijoy and Haraprasad created a misleading impression of Ananda Marga in the minds of the public. People developed peculiar ideas about the Margis, and hostile forces exploited this to the hilt to create a public misunderstanding about the Marga. This had a somewhat negative effect on the Marga's spread in Krishnanagar, and the Margis had to labor hard to remove the misconception. Out of concern some of them requested Sukhen to report the matter to Baba. So he went to Jamalpur and related to Baba what had happened to Haraprasad. Baba told Sukhen to instruct Haraprasad to meditate properly and assured him that he would be almost normal by the time Sukhen returned to

Krishnanagar. Indeed, when Sukhen arrived there he found a big change in Haraprasad. Soon he became completely normal to the great relief of the Margis and his family.

Although Bijoy was now normal, a new kind of problem arose for which his family members were entirely responsible. They prevented Bijoy from having any contact with the Margis and forced him to eat onion, garlic, and non-vegetarian food. They also did not allow him to do meditation, and this created a serious mental imbalance in Bijoy. Unable to tolerate the treatment he was receiving from his family, he attempted to commit suicide, causing great consternation in the family. About four months after returning from Amra, one Saturday afternoon, Bijoy's brother came to Sukhen and invited him to their house to see Bijoy immediately. Sukhen refused, saying that their mother did not like the Margis to meet him and was abusive to them if they went there. The brother explained that his mother had actually sent him to fetch Sukhen.

Reluctantly Sukhen agreed. When he reached Bijoy's house, he saw that Bijoy was looking dishevelled and was speaking incoherently. Upon inquiry, the family said that he had been completely normal for a few weeks after returning from Amra and had even started to go to court. Then suddenly one day he developed symptoms of mental imbalance. Sukhen could not understand what was wrong with Bijoy and asked him to write a letter to Baba about the matter.

Bijoy wrote, "Most reverent Baba, for the last few days I have again become abnormal. My whole family is disturbed due to my abnormal behavior. I am not able to attend court. It is the wish of my entire family that with your blessings, I will become normal again." Sukhen added a covering note, "Forwarded to the general secretary for your information and to communicate to Baba."

Since it was a Saturday evening, Sukhen said that he would post the letter on Monday. By that time more Margis had gathered at Bijoy's house. Sukhen told Bijoy's mother that he wanted to take Bijoy to stay with them for some days. By this time, the attitude of Bijoy's family had changed considerably and they felt that only the Margis could offer them a glimmer of hope, so they readily agreed.

Within a few minutes of joining the Margis, there was dramatic improvement in Bijoy. He stayed with them until late in the evening and for most of the next day, and they meditated together. By Sunday evening he had become completely normal. Bijoy revealed to Sukhen that he had lost his mental balance because he was prevented by his family from doing meditation and was being forced to eat non-vegetarian and other static food, which he was unable to digest. Sukhen strictly instructed the family members not to create any hindrance in his sadhana or feed him onions, garlic, meat, or fish, as they were static in nature and harmful for him. The family was by now ready to cooperate. From the following Monday Bijoy resumed going to court, and from then onwards his life became normal. His letter to Baba remained unsent, as his prayers seemed to have been answered the moment he wrote it.

Amra witnessed another miraculous event. Unlike the Bijoy episode which affected many Margis and non-Margis alike, this was the personal experience of a simple and devoted police officer. A couple of months before the Amra DMC, Baba invited the senior Margis visiting Jamalpur to attend the program at Amra. In fact, it was only one of two DMCs wherein Baba personally invited the Margis to attend. He told everyone that the DMC in Amra would be a very special one, so the Margis came from many parts of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and other neighboring states, as well as from Bengal.

Acharya Bhagavat, a low ranking police officer, was one of those who Baba personally invited. One day during his evening walk, Baba mentioned the Amra DMC to him. "Bhagavat, it will be a very special DMC and you should not miss it."

Bhagavat replied, "Baba, you will be speaking Bengali at Amra. You know that I don't understand any Bengali at all. What purpose will it serve, since I won't understand your speech?"

"Bhagavat, don't worry about that. You will be able to understand everything I say," said Baba reassuringly. Nityananda also invited Bhagavat to attend the DMC, as it was taking place in his village. On receiving Baba's assurance that he would be able to understand his speech, Bhagavat decided to attend. He was posted in Katihar in Northern Bihar at that time. Professor Indradev Gupta of Katihar also wanted to go to the DMC, as Baba had informed him that it would be a special one. Just as the date approached, his wife became very ill. However, in the afternoon before the commencement of the DMC program, Indradev was unable to resist his urge to attend. He told Bhagavat that if they did not start the journey by evening, they would miss the main program. He decided to leave his wife in the care of a boy from the neighborhood. Bhagavat had applied for leave from his police duty, and after much effort, he too had managed to secure one day's leave. In the evening both of them set off for Amra. Along the way Indradev repeatedly expressed concern about the health of his wife. However, he consoled himself by saying that Baba was there to take care of her.

They arrived in Amra on the day of the DMC. As soon as they arrived, they went to meet Baba. When Indradev got up after prostrating, Baba said, "Indradev, don't worry. Your wife has recovered and is now fine." Indradev felt greatly relieved to hear that.

Upon reaching Amra village, Bhagavat thought, "This is an interior place in Bengal, and Baba won't speak Hindi here. But he has assured me that I will understand everything. How will that be possible when I don't know any Bengali?"

As he got up after prostrating, Baba said reassuringly, "Bhagavat, don't worry. You will understand everything that I say in the DMC today."

During the DMC Bhagavat heard Baba speaking in Hindi, but he had some doubt about it as he saw the Bengali Margis paying keen attention, and from their gestures they seemed to be able to understand what he was saying. Curious, he asked Indradev Gupta who was taking notes, "What language is Baba speaking?"
