Indradev was surprised by such a question. "Are you not listening? What language do you expect him to speak in Bengal if not Bengali?" he replied, visibly annoyed at such a silly question.

Bhagavat twitched his ears in disbelief. He was clearly hearing Baba speaking in Hindi. To check if he was hearing correctly, he asked Indradev if Baba was speaking on such and such a topic. Indradev confirmed it. Still unable to believe that Baba was speaking Bengali, he asked some other people as well after the DMC was over. Everyone confirmed that Baba had spoken in Bengali during the discourse and had not uttered a word of Hindi.

After the program, Bhagavat went to Indradev to verify if what he had written in his notes was the same as what he had heard. To his surprise, everything tallied. He confided his strange experience to Acharya Raghunath, but Raghunath was initially skeptical about his claims. However, Bhagavat insisted that Baba had spoken in Hindi. Seeing the conviction with which he spoke, Raghunath felt that something strange might have taken place and decided to clarify the matter with Baba.

A few months later, during a visit to Jamalpur, he mentioned the incident to Baba during the Field Walk. Baba said, "Raghunath, what Bhagavat said is true. Do you know what happened? Bhagavat could not understand Bengali. I had assured him that he would be able to understand what I said during the DMC, so the sound waves of the Bengali words I spoke were converted into Hindi before they reached his ears, and Bhagavat heard my speech in Hindi. I could have employed another method to make him understand if I wished. I could have opened his intuitional mind a little bit and he would have developed the ability to understand Bengali. By developing the intuitional part of the mind, one can understand every language of the world."

Raghunath was amazed to hear Baba's clarification on this matter.

Just as Baba had assured the Margis, the Amra DMC was indeed a special experience for those who were privileged to attend it. The sacred memory of the unique events of those two days remained etched in their minds for a long time afterwards.

CHAPTER 29

# Krishnanagar Will Dance

Early in August 1958 Haraprasad and Sukhen went to Jamalpur to solicit Baba's help with the work in Krishnanagar. One evening during the Field Walk, Haraprasad said, "Baba, although Bijoy has now become completely normal, Ananda Marga has still not been able to overcome the negative publicity that the controversy around him created. The false accusations that were made against the Marga are still lingering in people's minds. It is affecting our prachar work, and we don't know what to do."

"The solution is simple," replied Baba. "Organize a DMC there and the atmosphere will change."

"Baba, DMC is an internal program among the Margis, so how will it erase the negative public view of the Marga?" asked Haraprasad. "Moreover, how is it possible to hold a DMC at a time when many people are hostile towards Ananda Marga? Some inimical forces may whip up mass hysteria against the Marga, and we will find it difficult to handle your security and that of the Margis attending the program."

"Don't worry about that. Just go ahead with the preparations for the DMC, and everything will be taken care of."

Haraprasad was still not convinced about the Margis' ability to hold a DMC. Then suddenly an idea came in his mind. He said, "Baba, we can hold the DMC if you give me the occult power you gave me during the Amrah DMC. Without that it will not be possible to hold a DMC in this situation."

"Hara, do you know better than me what is needed and what is not? Occult powers are not for worldly use as you think," replied Baba with a tinge of irritation in his voice. "Organize the DMC and even the ordinary people of Krishnanagar will have abnormal spiritual experiences. Krishnanagar will dance in ecstasy. Now go and consult the general secretary about the date for the DMC and then start the preparations immediately."

While returning from the Tiger's Grave Baba gave them further instructions. "Several hundred Margis will come from Bihar alone. In addition to that there will be the Margis from Bengal, the Northeast, Orissa, UP and a few from other places, which will make it the biggest gathering Ananda Marga has seen until now. This will be the first gathering of Margis from so many states. So your arrangements should take that into consideration. It will not be possible for you to provide free food for such a huge gathering, as has been the practice at all the DMCs until now. So charge them for their food, but give them free accommodation. And let those who want a private room pay for it." They took Baba's blessing by touching his feet. Just as he was about to enter his house, he turned around and said, "Krishnanagar will have my special blessing. This DMC will be remembered forever in the history of Ananda Marga."

### Resistance to Being Initiated

From the early days Krishnanagar was one of the most active units of the Marga in Bengal. Towards the end of 1955 Haraprasad was trained as an acharya. Soon after, Baba asked him to take leave from his job and go for prachar work. His duty was to develop Ananda Marga units in Calcutta and Krishnanagar. Haraprasad recalled that during their very first meeting in the accounts office in May 1950, Baba had asked him, "Do you know Sukhendranath Naik, Manas Mohan, Shyama Chand Ganguly, Anil Banerjee and Manoranjan Sen?" As they were all his close friends, he concluded that Baba had already selected them as disciples and had decided to start the work of the Marga in Krishnanagar by initiating them. All of them except Manoranjan Sen were initiated without much effort, and after some time Sukhendranath (Sukhen), Manas Mohan and Shyama Chand took training as acharyas.

However, Manoranjan Sen vehemently refused to take initiation despite the repeated efforts of Haraprasad, Sukhen and the others. Finally they gave up trying, thinking that if Baba had indeed selected him as a disciple, Manoranjan would certainly learn meditation one day and become a Margi.

Since his college days Manoranjan had been influenced by leftist ideas and had strong aversion to the dogmas propagated by the religions. He considered spirituality to be an extension of these dogmatic religions. Despite his reluctance Sukhen and Haraprasad continued to persuade him to take initiation, but none of their efforts to convince him bore fruit.

At the beginning of 1957 Manoranjan came down with a severe attack of sciatica. Sukhen advised him to meditate, perform yoga exercises and observe a sentient diet, saying that these practices would surely cure him. But Manoranjan did not give any credence to his words, as he felt that Sukhen was exploiting his illness to pressure him to take initiation. He told Sukhen that he did not believe that meditation could cure a disease and that curing a disease required medicine. However, after he took a variety of different medicines and three months of bed rest on medical advice, there was no improvement in his condition. Finally, in desperation, Manoranjan invited his friend, Sukhen, to see if his mantra and tantra would really cure the disease. Sukhen taught him meditation and certain yogic exercises. He also advised him to follow some dietary restrictions. Within a week Manoranjan's health improved dramatically and he was able to walk without much pain. As he continued to make progress, Sukhen and Haraprasad suggested that he should go to Jamalpur to see the guru.

A few days later, accompanied by Sukhen and Haraprasad, Manoranjan set off for Jamalpur. The next day they had the opportunity to go on Field Walk. Baba was striding out at his usual fast pace, and Manoranjan had to struggle to keep up with him. As they sat down on the Tiger's Grave, he was racked with acute spasms of pain. After spending an hour discussing various things with the other Margis, Baba got up to leave. Suddenly the pain became so acute that Manoranjan could not even stand up. He struggled to follow, ending up in still more pain. Exasperated and in agony, he said to Sukhen, "It is better to die than to live with such terrible pain. I thought that the asanas and meditation had almost cured me, but the pain has become unbearable."

Sukhen tried to assist him to walk. Baba, who was already several steps ahead, stopped and asked them to come quickly. Leaning heavily on Sukhen, Manoranjan walked towards Baba with faltering steps. "Tonight Haraprasad will massage the affected area and then you will be cured," Baba said and walked away. With great difficulty Manoranjan managed to walk all the way to the jagrti.

Later that night Haraprasad massaged the affected area of Manoranjan's leg. Seeing his amateurish efforts, Manoranjan grew skeptical. He asked, "Hara, have you had any training in massage or did Baba tell you which areas to massage to cure sciatica?"

Haraprasad said, "No, I don't know anything. I am massaging you just because Baba asked me to do it."

"Hara, I don't mean to offend you. But I have been massaged by professionally trained masseurs, and it did not bring any result. So what benefit will I get from you simply pressing my body? The problem is deep-rooted and your random efforts will not cure it."

"Mano, you should understand that it will be the grace of Baba that will cure you and not my ability to massage. Baba knows that I don't have any idea about massage. Even so, he said that you would be cured if I massaged you. Do you know what that means? It means that Baba has already graced you. He wants to make it appear as if it is my massage that has cured you and not his supernatural power. When you were with Baba the pain also recurred by his desire so that he could grace you. So now please relax and let me continue to massage you in my amateurish way."

Manoranjan stopped protesting and allowed Haraprasad to continue massaging. After a few minutes he fell asleep. When he woke up the next morning after a sound sleep, the first thing he noticed was that the pain had completely disappeared. Miraculously his sciatica never came back. Manoranjan returned from Jamalpur a changed man. He became a great devotee of Baba and started to work actively for the Marga in Krishnanagar. Shortly after his return he was made the unit secretary of Krishnanagar. Like Manoranjan Sen many Margis of Krishnanagar had their personal experiences of Baba's unbounded grace that helped to fortify their spiritual life, and Krishnanagar soon grew into a strong center of Ananda Marga.

### The Dancing Procession

Greatly inspired by Baba's assurance that the Krishnanagar DMC would be remembered in the history of Ananda Marga, Haraprasad and Sukhen discussed the preparations for the program with Pranay. It was fixed for the full moon day in October, which fell on the 25th and 26th of the month.

Baba personally invited all the Margis who visited him in Jamalpur to attend the Krishnanagar DMC, which he assured them would be a special one for everyone. This DMC and the one held in Amra were the only ones for which Baba personally invited the Margis. He formulated a set of rules to be followed at this and all subsequent DMCs.

The news that the Krishnanagar DMC would be a special one spread amongst the Margis like wildfire. They came from all over Bengal, Bihar, Orissa and Uttar Pradesh and even from some far-flung areas of the Northeast. It was the first time ever that such a large number of Margis had gathered in one place to attend a DMC.

On the 24th of October Baba arrived in Krishnanagar by train well after sunset. More than a thousand people had gathered at the railway station, and the municipal commissioner, Mohan Kali Biswas, was also there to receive Baba on behalf of the town. As everyone waited for the arrival of the train, some devotional songs of Rabindranath Tagore were sung, spiritually charging the atmosphere at the station.

Bindeshvari was his usual self, touching the foreheads of those who came near him and spiritually vibrating them. Seeing this strange sight, the municipal commissioner also approached him. Bindeshvari gently tapped his forehead. The commissioner felt a strong current pass through his body and sat down on a nearby bench with tears streaming down his face. As Baba alighted from the train, Haraprasad, Sukhen, Manoranjan and several others garlanded him amid loud shouts of 'Parama Pita Baba Ki, Jai' [Victory to Baba the Supreme Father] and 'Yogeshvar Shri Shri Anandamurtiji Ki, Jai' [Victory to Shri Shri Anandamurti, the Lord of the yogis.] Pranay then asked one of the Margis to collect the garlands the people had brought.

Suresh, a student from Patna, recalled the unusual experience of the Margis. "As Baba alighted from the train, a strong devotional wave suddenly enveloped the entire platform, and several Margis started to cry uncontrollably. Many of the onlookers wondered at the strange sight and some curious ones inquired why the Margis were crying."

As Baba walked to the exit surrounded by the Margis, the commissioner, who was still in trance, remained sitting on the platform bench holding the packet with the garland he had brought for him, oblivious of the commotion going on all around him. Baba took his seat in the car, and the Margis lined up behind it. Haraprasad had arranged for a band to play some devotional songs of the great saint, Mirabai, and the Margis danced and sang the Harinama kirtana popularised by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu.

As the procession wound through the streets of Krishnanagar, many of the onlookers could not restrain themselves and joined in the singing, drawn by the strong devotional vibration. Arrangements had been made for Baba to stay at the jagrti and all the available halls, schools and lodges had been booked for the Margis. By the time the procession reached the town hall where the function was to be held, the crowd had swelled to nearly double its

original size. There was a short Tattva Sabha for those who were curious to learn more about Ananda Marga. Again the next morning several groups of Margis held several rounds of group discussions. Hundreds of people showed interest in learning meditation. All the available acharyas who could speak Bengali were busy initiating those who wanted to learn meditation.

By evening a huge crowd of over five thousand people had gathered in front of the town hall to see Baba and receive his blessings. The number of people was many times more than what the hall could accommodate and they were deeply disappointed when they were told that only the Margis would be issued gate passes to attend the program.

Before Baba left for the town hall, news reached Pranay about the huge crowd that had gathered there. Worried, he summoned Sukhen and gave him the task of ensuring that nobody touched Baba's feet unless he himself permitted it. Explaining the problem he said, "You are aware that Baba has the practice of blessing all those who touch his feet, and in the process he will absorb their negative samskaras. If people who have a desire to be cured of a disease or relieved of any other misfortune touch his feet, Baba will certainly bless them and take upon himself their samskaras, whether or not they are Margis. Later he will suffer from all the negative samskaras he has taken upon himself. So we always take every precaution to prevent even the Margis from touching Baba's feet unless he permits them to do so. So we will have to ensure that, come what may, no one is allowed to touch Baba's feet without his permission. I am entrusting this important task to you."

Sensing the devotional mood of the crowd at the town hall, it was going to be an impossible task for not only Sukhen but even for all the Margis together to prevent the surging crowd from touching Baba's feet. He therefore took a couple of Margis into confidence and asked them to position themselves at the back entrance and open the gate only when Baba arrived. To avoid drawing the attention of the crowd, Sukhen brought Baba in a rickshaw and entered through the back gate unnoticed.

As Baba took his seat inside the hall, he called Shiva Shankar and asked him what the noise outside was about. Shiva Shankar informed him that a large crowd had gathered, all eager to attend the program. In response, Baba directed the Margis to open all the doors and windows and to set up loudspeakers outside to enable the public to listen to his speech. Several non-Margis managed to squeeze into the crammed hall, while the rest sat down where they were and tried to catch a glimpse of Baba through the open doors and windows.

After the devotional songs and kirtan, which many members of the public participated in, Baba gave his Renaissance Universal speech. The topic was "The impossibility of peaceful co-existence of two opposing forces." "Just as light and darkness cannot coexist, vice and virtue, good and bad also cannot coexist. Their fight is a constant one. It is a never-ending struggle. So anyone who talks about the peaceful coexistence of opposing forces is merely trying to gain cheap popularity. One of them will have to give way to the other. In the struggle between good and bad, virtue and vice, one will ultimately disappear; one will be expelled by the other. You are all sadhakas; you must remember that yours is a never-ending struggle against all types of meanness, crudeness and depraving tendencies.

"A person who has devotion for God cannot be a mute witness to the wrongdoings of those who exploit and oppress the people. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was the embodiment of struggle against social evils. He opposed discrimination against people on the basis of high and low caste and embraced even those considered untouchable, giving them love and respect. He also vehemently opposed the religious exploitation of the so-called custodians of the gods. Because of this, he had to face tremendous opposition from the perpetrators of religious exploitation who inhumanly discriminated against the lower echelons of society. Finally, due to his struggle against the evil forces in society, he had to pay the ultimate price."

### Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's Disappearance

Later that evening, Baba went for his customary evening walk. Sukhen recalled what Baba said that day. "Baba went to the riverbank of the Jalangi River near our present jagrti accompanied by seven or eight Margis. He was in a pleasant mood. It was a very memorable occasion as he disclosed many little known facts about the history of Krishnanagar and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. He started by talking about various places in Nadia District. We were spellbound to hear one amazing fact after another flowing from his mouth. Indeed he seemed to be a fountain of knowledge. In the course of the discussion, Baba described a very old tree found in the village of Bagchi Jamsherpur and said that it was three thousand years old and that there was a similar tree of about the same age in the botanical park in Howrah. He also discussed the history of Krishnanagar and commented, 'Krishna Chandra, the King of Krishnanagar, was not from the warrior class as was generally the case with Hindu kings. He came from a Brahmin family of Rarh. He did a lot of good to society. As a result his fame spread far and wide, even beyond the borders of Bengal. He brought many expert sweet makers from the neighboring district of Burdwan and built up the sweet industry by inspiring them to prepare new varieties of sweets. He also brought many shellac artists from Ilambazar in Birbhum District and settled them in Ghurni, Nadia. Today Nadia has a worldwide reputation for clay-modeling due to the patronage of King Krishna Chandra. In those days most townships developed in a haphazard manner, but King Krishna Chandra employed Allal Dastur Pir, a city architect of Bengal, to build the town of Krishnanagar in a planned way. Three places, Ghurni, Goyari and Krishnanagar, together became the cultural hub of Bengal at the time. During the reign of Maharaja Krishna Chandra some sealing-wax artisans were brought from Ilambazaar to reside in Ghurni. They were the forefathers of Krishnanagar's renowned modern-day clay sculptors.'

"Baba suddenly changed subjects and began to discuss Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. 'Nadia district with Krishnanagar as its headquarters is the land where Chaitanya Mahaprabhu was born and brought up. He began his mission of mass public kirtan here. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu introduced many new ideas in both the practical and social spheres. He opposed casteism and embraced people of all castes and hues, breaking all barriers of discrimination. As a result he met with intense opposition from the fundamentalists, who went as far as to threaten his life. In his God-intoxicated state he spiritually vibrated everyone who came in his contact. People ran after him, madly dancing, crying, singing and laughing in ecstatic joy; such were the devotional feelings he aroused in them. In Ananda Marga this divine flow of Brahma is embedded in the different lessons of our meditation. That is why you see Margis cry, sing and dance with profound spiritual joy; this happens in greater measure in our spiritual congregation. This will happen far more in the future as you all advance steadily towards the blissful Macrocosmic Entity.

'Because Mahaprabhu was constantly in a God-intoxicated state, he was unable to hate anyone, even those who attacked or criticized him. He was a genuine humanist and a true sadvipra. Sadvipras ensure that those who do dreadful crimes are punished, but they never hate them or deprive them of food or the basic necessities of life, because sadvipras are humanists. When a low caste Muslim, Haridas, became ill, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu found it impossible to remain indifferent to him. He took Haridas in his arms and nursed him tenderly, thus showing his respect for human values.

'Haridas did not want Mahaprabhu to touch him as he was from a low caste and an untouchable in the eyes of the caste-ridden society of the day. Seeing this, Mahaprabhu would say, "Haridas, you are such a great devotee, you have so much devotion in your heart that I just want to touch you so I can make myself holier. You are so full of devotion that you can make the whole universe holy. Devotion has tremendous power, much more than knowledge or action.

'Later Mahaprabhu moved to Puri, which at that time was a hub of religious exploitation. In response to those who were perpetuating the oppression of untouchables, Mahaprabhu openly declared, "An untouchable is not an untouchable if he takes the name of Lord Krishna. A Brahman is not a Brahman if he is dishonest." This infuriated the Brahmin priests of Puri because they were all dishonest and fleeced the people who came to the temple.

'Mahaprabhu's teachings were also a threat to the exploitation of the Muslim mullahs, as quite a few Muslims were joining the mass kirtans and were being socially awakened. The mullahs were therefore afraid of losing control over them, so the orthodox Muslims united with the orthodox Brahmins against Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Although Mahaprabhu had been born into a well-known Brahmin family, he suffered many insults because of his opposition to casteism and the religious exploitation perpetrated by the so-called custodians of religion. Despite this he steadfastly stuck to his ideology.'

"At that point one of us asked, 'Baba, in your discourse a while ago, you said that Mahaprabhu had to pay the ultimate price due to his struggle against social evil. What is the truth about Mahaprabhu's disappearance? It was claimed that his body and soul had merged into the idol of Lord Krishna.'

"Baba stopped for a while and became silent. Then he continued in a sombre tone, 'Mahaprabhu's teaching of humanism and love for God and his ceaseless railing against all kinds of religious exploitation angered those who were profiting from spreading dogmatic ideas and exploiting the people. The religious bigots were infuriated by the teachings of Mahaprabhu and threatened him with dire consequences if he did not stop spreading his 'harmful' ideas among the common people. Like any true spiritualist, Mahaprabhu was fearless and paid no heed to their threats. One day when he was in a devotional trance, they murdered him, tied his dead body in a gunny bag and threw it in the ocean. Then they concocted the fanciful story that his soul, along with his body, had merged into idol of Lord Jagannath (another name of Lord Krishna), the deity in the temple. It was a very cunning story because if anyone doubted it, the priests would be able to claim that they did not believe in the greatness of Mahaprabhu and the divine powers of Lord Krishna. Even while his life was ebbing away, Mahaprabhu's thoughts were fixed on Lord Krishna, and after his death he became one with Krishna and attained salvation, whereas those who were responsible for this gruesome act had to suffer terrible retribution at the hands of Nature for their heinous crime. All of them were born in lower forms of life and, except for one, they have yet to get a human body again. One of them repented his actions and so, after several lives, he has again attained a human form. The others are still incarnated as various lower forms of life.' Seeing how grave Baba had become while talking about the death of Mahaprabhu, we did not probe any further."

### Releasing the Hladini Force

In Krishnanagar the flow of devotion continued unabated the next day as well. The gathering for the DMC that evening was much larger than on the previous evening. Sukhen again brought Baba inside through the back entrance unnoticed.

Many of the townspeople felt an exceptional devotional vibration throughout Baba's stay in Krishnanagar. On the DMC night it reached a climax. After the devotional songs Baba raised his hands and crossed both index fingers in a special mudra, whereupon everyone in the hall started to sing kirtan and dance in joy. The devotional fervor was indescribable. Later Gopen Mukharjee led the singing of the Harinam Kirtan and quickly fell into a state of divine ecstasy. He was soon followed by many others. Acharya Sakaldev, the well-built lawyer from Muzaffarpur, and some others carried outside those who had fallen into a spiritual trance to prevent them from being trampled upon by others who were still dancing in ecstasy, oblivious of their surroundings. They were laid in a vacant space outside the hall. Many women also fell over in divine ecstasy. They were then moved to a corner of the hall by female volunteers.

The devotional songs, ecstatic dancing and crying continued for some time, but once Baba started his discourse there was pin-drop silence both inside and outside the hall. Baba's discourse was on "Samskara and the Attainment of Liberation." He described the kinds of samskaras that could be accrued through the different activities that a person performs and through the environment that he or she is brought up in. He also discussed different ways of liberating oneself from the bondages created by those samskaras.

Sukhen also helped to remove those who had fallen into a trance from the hall. He described the scene outside:

"I was walking around outside, trying to gauge the reaction of the public and to check if everything was in order. I was astonished to see respectable lawyers, college lecturers and doctors sitting on the grass listening attentively to Baba's talk. At the end of the discourse, devotional songs were sung. I don't know what happened after that, but suddenly we all felt a powerful spiritual wave. Immediately everyone inside the hall started to sing kirtan and dance in ecstasy once again, and the Margis and the general public outside joined in. The urge to join them was so strong that I had to forcibly restrain myself, as I had the duty to oversee the program."

Asit,[^1] a local student, participated in the program from outside the hall. Recalling the scene that evening, he said, "After the guru left, some of us peeped in through the window and saw that most of the people were lying on the floor. I thought that they had become unconscious, but when I looked again, I saw that some were conscious and were crying, while others were making a strange guttural sound of 'hum, hum, hum.' We thought that they were in some kind of pain or had gone mad. We switched on our flashlights to check more closely and saw a strange serenity in their faces. For some inexplicable reason, just looking at their faces gave us much joy. Among them were several who were not Margis. Some of them later told me that they had felt an incredible feeling of bliss at that time. This inspired me to learn meditation, as I too wanted to have a taste of such blissful experiences."

The next morning Baba pleasantly surprised everyone by declaring that he would give darshan at ten o'clock. The Margis assembled in the town hall well before the scheduled time and even before Baba arrived some started singing devotional songs, while others danced and cried in ecstasy. The gathering was almost entirely composed of Margis, as the public had not been informed about this impromptu program. When Baba took his seat on the dais, Sukhen offered him a garland while a devotional song of Rabindranath Tagore was sung:

> "*Ananda loke mangala loke virajo satya sundara.*"
> (You permeate the abode of bliss and benevolence, O eternal, beautiful one.)

The enchanting melody and the deeply devotional meaning of the song created a tremendous vibration in the hall. Gopen stood up and started swaying to the music. He was soon joined by many others. More songs followed and the entire hall erupted in ecstatic utterances of "hum, hum." Many were crying while others were sitting in the lotus posture with tears of ecstasy streaming down their cheeks.

That morning Nityananda reported everything to Baba and remarked that it seemed as if during the Harinam Kirtan he had been making the devotees dance to the beat of the cosmic rhythm. Baba smiled and said, "Do you know, the great devotee Narada asked God a question about Harinam Kirtan. 'O God, where do you live?' In reply God said, 'I do not live in heaven or in the hearts of the yogis, Narada. I live where my devotees sing my name.'"

Although Baba's program in Krishnanagar was supposed to be restricted to the Margis, it created a great stir among the general public as well. Later that evening a huge crowd showed up at the railway station to see Baba off. The volunteers struggled hard to prevent people from falling at Baba's feet in obeisance. The Margis and members of the public sang and danced

[^1]: Later Asit dedicated his life and joined the monastic order, and was given the name Amritananda

while tears streamed down their faces. Many of those who were interviewed recalled that nothing like that had ever been seen in Krishnanagar either before or since the program. Before boarding the train, he said, "I am leaving you all physically, but I will remain with you in the deepest core of your being for eternity."

As Baba had indicated to Haraprasad and Sukhen, the entire town of Krishnanagar had danced to the melodies and devotional vibrations his divine presence had inspired. The hostility that had pervaded the town before his arrival had vanished like mist that disappears with the rising sun, and the entire atmosphere was transformed in a way that the Margis had never anticipated. That was the only time when Baba had unleashed such blissful vibrations over an entire town during a Marga program.

Although the Margis were blessed with similar devotional experiences on several other occasions, the Krishnanagar DMC remained etched in the memories of those who attended it. No one had ever witnessed a DMC like it in their lives. It appeared as if the whole town had been flooded with an intense devotional flow. Just as Baba had assured them, it had been a unique experience, the sweet memories of which would remain with them forever. For some of them the ecstasy they experienced during the program lasted for several months.

As the Margis returned home afterwards, one question lingered in their minds. How had it happened that everyone, including many members of the public, had sung and danced and gone into ecstasy during Baba's presence in Krishnanagar? Over the next few months this was a hot topic of discussion amongst the Margis. They all had different opinions about it, but no one had a conclusive answer.

On the 25ᵗʰ of December 1958 a large number of Margis gathered in Jamalpur. Many of them had come to help with the construction of the new jagrti, which was to be inaugurated four days later. In his darshan that day Baba talked about the forces of attraction and repulsion. "The Supreme Creative Principle has two forces. One takes people closer to the Macrocosmic Nucleus and one leads them away from it. The force that leads people away from the Macrocosmic Nucleus is the centrifugal force called *Avidya Maya*, and the one that takes them closer is the centripetal force of *Vidya Maya*. Each of these forces has two aspects. The two aspects of *Avidya* are *vikshepa* and *avarani*. Due to the effect of vikshepa, debasing tendencies take root in people's minds, which lead them away from the Macrocosmic Nucleus. Under the influence of Avarani, they think that when they commit a sin, nobody is watching. They forget that there is an entity that watches everything that happens in the entire creation and that nothing can remain hidden from that Supreme Entity. The influence of avarani is like a black curtain that comes down between an individual and the Macrocosmic Nucleus, preventing him from seeing things in their true perspective. The two aspects of *Vidya* are *samvit* and *hladini*. All of a sudden a person who is engaged in bad actions feels, 'No, I shouldn't do all these things. From now on I should become a good man. I must become a spiritualist. I must not allow any degrading thoughts to enter my mind.' Such an idea comes to him suddenly. This change of thinking is brought about by the samvit force of Vidya Maya. When a person makes such a resolution under the influence of samvit, he obtains the Supreme Grace, and this accelerates his progress towards the Supreme Nucleus. Hladini is also called *Radhika Shakti* and it can establish a person in *radha bhava*, the highest type of devotion. Suppose the force of hladini increases even a little, the person will be immersed in divine ecstasy and in that state he cannot but sing and dance uninhibitedly. If even a wee bit of the hladini force is applied to a large gathering of people, everyone will sing and dance in divine bliss. Now do you all understand what happened in Krishnanagar?" asked Baba with a sweet, mystic smile. Many of the Margis present had attended the program there and were pleasantly surprised by Baba's unexpected explanation of the events that had taken place.

Baba also released the hladini shakti on several occasions such as organizational meetings, DMCs and other spiritual gatherings. Everyone present would go wild with divine

ecstasy. Then Baba would say, "I have increased the spiritual force only a wee bit. Even that makes you so ecstatic. Do you know what would happen if I increased it further? You would all become spiritually intoxicated and would not be able to do any work."

That evening, Rajmohan Mishra, an executive engineer in the Public Works Department of Bihar, was with Baba during his Field Walk. As they entered the field and walked towards the Tiger's Grave, he asked somewhat hesitantly, "Baba, is it not possible to increase the hladini force in such a way that people will be attracted to spirituality en masse? Wouldn't that assist the spread of the Marga?"

"See, Rajmohan, if I want, in less than the blink of an eye I can engulf the whole world in spiritual bliss. But that is not the way to spread your ideology. You should never wish for it to happen so easily. What a person gains without effort does not last long. Ananda Marga will be established with a lot of struggle and sacrifice, and that alone will enable it to endure. Of course a time will come when both the samvit and hladini forces will be augmented by divine grace and that will drench the whole world in ecstasy. But all of you will not be around to see that day. Those who live today will not see that day, and those who see that day will feel very sad that they were not here today." With these words Baba looked at Rajmohan with a mysterious smile and walked towards the Tiger's Grave followed by the rest of the Margis.

CHAPTER 30

# The First Struggle

By the middle of 1958 the number of new people coming to Jamalpur attracted by Baba's extraordinary personality was increasing exponentially. The small Rampur Colony quarters that had served as the jagrti and headquarters of the Marga was no longer able to accommodate the rapidly increasing number of Margis.

For these reasons Baba told Pranay to look for a building large enough to accommodate the growing number of Margis visiting Jamalpur. Although he understood the need, Pranay was at a loss as to how to raise the funds for the building, as most of the Margis were simple villagers on a low income who had barely enough money to maintain their families. In addition, they were already supporting the various activities of the Marga, such as paying the jagrti rent, arranging regular activities to propagate the Ananda Marga ideology and organizing the monthly Dharma Maha Chakra, among others. So they could not be expected to contribute anything. Realizing the acute difficulty he would face in collecting the large amount of funds that were required for the construction of a new jagrti, Pranay delayed the project as long as possible. To solve the problems faced by the neighbors, he decided to vacate the present building and rent another one instead for the time being.

While Pranay wrestled with the problem of how to finance the construction of a jagrti in Jamalpur, the Margis of Bhagalpur had already built theirs. It was the first property the Marga owned and was inaugurated by Baba on the 10th of August 1958. He then inaugurated the first Abha Seva Sadan medical camp which was held in the same jagrti premises and provided free medical care for the poor. A small library and reading room for the public was also opened there. A grand DMC was organized to mark the occasion.

### Welcoming Struggle

Soon after returning to Jamalpur from Bhagalpur, Baba directed Pranay to vacate the Rampur Colony jagrti and move operations to a larger rented building outside the colony, while preparations were made to build their own place. He gave Pranay less than a week to do it. However, finding a building for rent in Jamalpur big enough to accommodate the needs of the jagrti was an onerous task indeed. There was a severe shortage of suitable buildings as the railway employees coming from other areas had taken up all the available accommodation. After an exhaustive search for about a month, the only residential building that could be found was an old, ramshackle structure in a by-lane near the market. Although it was not at all suitable for a jagrti, arrangements were quickly made to rent it.

In the meanwhile, Baba began to ratchet up pressure on Pranay to look for a piece of land to buy. Despite several days of searching, Pranay made no progress, mainly because no funds were available for the purchase of the land. At that time the land prices in and around Jamalpur were relatively high. When this was reported to Baba, he instructed Pranay to look for land in the vicinity of Olipur. So Pranay entrusted the task to Ramkhilavan, a resident of the locality.

Within a few days Ramkhilavan informed Pranay about a property belonging to a businessman from Monghyr which might be available cheaply because it had been forcibly occupied by a local thug called Bachchu Mandal. Bachchu had paid a small deposit for the property but had later defaulted on the remaining payment. Although the agreement was annulled and the deposit returned, Bachchu continued to stake his claim to the property and threatened to kill the businessman if he tried to reclaim it. Not wanting to get into a direct conflict with Bachchu, the businessman was trying to sell off the property cheaply. Ramkhilavan asked Pranay to ask Baba if it was proper to buy a piece of land which had so

The First Struggle

many problems. Pranay replied that Baba must have been alluding to that particular property when he asked him to look for cheap land in Olipur. So there was no need to refer the matter to Baba, and efforts should be made to buy it. Then in a lighter mood he remarked, "Maybe Baba wants to prepare us to build a stronger Ananda Marga by welcoming struggle in the early stages itself."

Ramkhilavan contacted the landowner who offered it at a bargain price. When the news was communicated to Pranay, he managed to raise the funds from the Margis and in the second week of October registered the property. Having dealt with the legal aspects, the Margis now had to find ways to evict Bachchu. Dasharath suggested trying to win him over by inviting him to lay the foundation stone for the jagrti. So the Margis approached Bachchu with this proposal. The attempt backfired, however, as Bachchu threatened them with dire consequences if they tried to enter the land. Pranay was in a dilemma and brought the matter to Baba's notice. Baba's response was firm and unyielding. He directed Pranay to ignore the threats and to occupy the land by force if necessary, as Bachchu had illegally occupied it and would not listen to reason. Baba's strong response put a lot of pressure on Pranay.

In the meantime, Ramkhilavan discovered that an adjoining property that once belonged to a Muslim family who had migrated to Pakistan after the Partition would soon be auctioned off.

Since the registered property was insufficient for the new jagrti, Pranay brought the matter to Baba's notice. Baba directed him to immediately contact the official concerned in the Evacuee Land Office in Patna instead of waiting for the auction to take place. He said that the officer was a spiritually minded person and would be willing to fix a moderate price for the property even without calling for an auction, provided that it was used for spiritual purposes. So Pranay went to Patna along with Dasharath and the lawyer Vaidyanath. They explained to the officer-in-charge their intention of buying the evacuee property for an ashram. Upon hearing that the property was to be used for an ashram, he readily agreed to give it to them for a mere 1500 rupees, which was considerably cheaper than the auction price. Once the registration was completed in the beginning of November, Baba ordered Pranay to take immediate possession of both plots of land and to erect a compound wall around the land.

### Applying Stambhan Kriya

While Pranay grappled with the problem of evicting Bachchu, Dasharath brought the disturbing news that Bachchu had built a temple on the land and had started performing daily worship at the shrine. He was alarmed by Bachchu's cunning ploy. He knew that if the temple became functional, it would be impossible to evict Bachchu from the land, as neither the court nor the administration would want to disturb a place of worship. Pranay also grew very worried on hearing this news, as taking possession of the land was becoming far more complicated than he had anticipated. A couple of days later Dasharath decided to visit the land to verify the facts. At the sight of Dasharath, Bachchu's son, Taradas Mandal, who was a little inebriated, came running towards him with a *bujhali* in his hand. Shouting menacingly, he raised the *bujhali* to strike Dasharath. Realizing the grave danger he was in, Dasharath froze in fright. He involuntarily raised his umbrella to protect himself and closed his eyes and ideated on Baba, expecting to be hit at any moment. After a few seconds when nothing happened, he opened his eyes and to his amazement saw that Taradas was standing frozen like a statue with his hand raised, holding the *bujhali*. One of the shocked onlookers shouted, "Master Sahib, please leave immediately. They are criminals and will stop at nothing to hold onto the land."

Stunned by the incident, Dasharath turned around and swiftly walked away. He went to the jagrti where he saw Baba sitting in deep discussion with some Margis. As he prostrated,

Baba smiled and said sweetly in Angika, "Today the Master Sahib's head would have been split in two if I had not intervened and applied *stambhan kriya*[^1] and made him immobile."

Tears welled up in Dasharath's eyes. He said, "Yes, Baba, it was your grace alone that saved me today. Otherwise Tara would surely have killed me. When he raised the bujhali to hit me, I didn't know what to do and just froze. So I closed my eyes and thought of you. When I opened them again after a few moments I saw that he was standing still like a statue." Smiling, Baba nodded his head affirmatively. Dasharath then reported the existence of the makeshift temple on the plot of land.

When he heard this Baba grew annoyed with Pranay, "That's why I told you that taking possession of the land should brook no delay, as delays would only complicate the matter. So I want you to immediately take over the place."

### Never Surrender to Fear

The next day was a Sunday, the 16th of November. Pranay urgently summoned a meeting of some senior Margis. Asthana, Shyam Narayan, Ramtanuk, Dr. Amarnath, Jitendra Tyagi and a few others attended. Pranay briefed them about the situation, particularly the threat they faced in their efforts to retake the land. He then told them, "Baba wants us to forcibly occupy the land."

On this point Sukumar opined, "Considering the attitude of Bachchu and his sons, it will certainly end in violence and injury to the Margis and result in a criminal case being filed against both sides. This will bring bad publicity to the Marga and demoralize the Margis. So forcible occupation of the land will only complicate matters further. Instead I would suggest that we immediately approach the court to order his eviction. While it will cause some delay, it is nevertheless the best option that we have."

Some of those present supported Sukumar, while others disagreed. As the discussion continued, Baba suddenly walked in. Taking his seat, he asked, "So Pranay, I hope that steps have been planned to take possession of our land immediately?"

"Baba, some people think that we should move the case to the court and get Bachchu evicted," replied Pranay hesitantly.

"Go to court! Don't you know that will mean years of delay? We can't wait for years." Then, raising his voice, Baba roared, "If you are all afraid, I will go and take possession of the land myself."

He then got up and walked towards the door. That spurred everyone into action. Some of them caught hold of his feet, pleading with him not to go. They promised that they would do whatever was necessary to take immediate possession of the land.

About fifteen Margis, led by Nityananda, volunteered for the job. Included in the group were Virendra Asthana, the assistant collector of customs, Shyam Narayan Srivastava, divisional traffic superintendent of railways, Dr. Amarnath Chakravarthy, advocate Ramtanuk Singh, Jitendra Tyagi the businessman and a few Margis from Jamalpur.

Suresh, a Margi student from Bhagalpur studying in Patna, was travelling home to Bhagalpur to attend the local Chatth festival that evening. As the train drew near Jamalpur, he had a sudden urge to have Baba's *darshan*. He decided to have Baba's *darshan*. So he got off the train in Jamalpur and went to the jagrti. He arrived just as the Margis were preparing to leave for Olipur to oust Bachchu from the land. Without hesitation he joined the group.

When the unarmed Margis entered the property, Bachchu and his two sons confronted them armed with sticks. A fiery argument erupted between Nityananda and Bachchu over the right to the land. As the verbal duel intensified, Bachchu and his sons raised their sticks aggressively and threatened to assault the Margis unless they left the place forthwith. Unprepared for a physical confrontation, some of the Margis backed off while others

[^1]: It is an occult power which, when applied, makes a person immobile

continued to argue. Seeing that some of them were in retreat, Bachchu was emboldened and became more aggressive. The fear was infectious and the other Margis also started to withdraw. Encouraged by this, Bachchu and his sons started to pelt the retreating Margis with stones. Suresh, who was the last one to pull back, was hit below his eye by a stone. The force of the blow broke his glasses, and his face started to bleed profusely. The others managed to escape unhurt. Dr. Amarnath immediately took Suresh to a nearby dispensary, gave him first aid and applied some medicine to his wound. He then took him to the railway guesthouse where he, Asthana and Shyam Narayan were staying.

The other Margis, shocked by the aggressive behavior of Bachchu and his sons, returned to the jagrti. Just as they entered the jagrti they saw Baba in a furious mood. Before they could say anything, he scolded them severely for their cowardice in retreating at the mere sound of Bachchu’s verbal threats. He said that this was just Bachchu’s psychological tactic to scare them and that he was emboldened by seeing them retreat in fear. That was why he and his sons had become more aggressive and thrown stones at them. He taunted them saying that they should wear *saris* and bangles like women and instead send the womenfolk to face Bachchu and his gang. Baba was also furious at them for leaving behind young Suresh to face the brunt of Bachchu’s offensive alone.

Baba then stressed the need for courage in individual and collective life. “It may happen that you are tormented by someone in your personal life and tolerate everything out of fear. If one day you summon up all your courage to oppose that person, you will find that the tyrant retreats in ignominy. Similarly, under the spell of fear, one community might allow itself to be exploited by another community. But if the exploited community turns against the exploiters, the tyrants will take to their heels. There is a great need for courage. Never surrender to fear in individual or collective life.”

Kranti, Ramkhilavan’s teenage niece, could not bear to see Baba so upset, and prompted by his words, stood up and offered to help, “Baba, if you permit, I will go and recover the land.”

Baba appreciated her courageous spirit but declined her request and directed Pranay to summon several Margis who worked in the police force and ordered them to devise a plan to evict Bachchu without delay. They included ex-police inspector Kedarnath Sharma from Ranchi, Bihar Military Police (BMP) officers Chandranath from Bhagalpur, Kishun Singh from Muzaffarpur and deputy superintendent of police Rambahadur Singh from Barhi, as well as some other Margi officers of the BMP and the regular police force.

### Curing the Wound by a Touch

In the evening when Suresh saw that Asthana, Shyam Narayan and Amarnath were preparing to accompany Baba for his evening Field Walk, he got up to accompany them. As the injury he had sustained in the fracas with Bachchu was severe, they advised him to rest. They were afraid that Baba would be furious with them if he saw the extent of the swelling on his face. But Suresh was adamant about going for the evening walk with Baba. As anticipated, Baba was still very upset with everyone except Suresh. He again scolded them for their cowardice in turning tail and running away from the fight with Bachchu. As he continued to admonish the Margis, he turned to Suresh and affectionately inquired, “How are you, Suresh?” As he spoke to Suresh, he deliberately avoided looking at the other Margis.

“I have severe pain in my body, Baba. The wound is also hurting a lot.”

Baba showed his utter disapproval of the Margis’ cowardly behavior by instructing Asthana and the others to massage Suresh’s body. Suresh felt embarrassed that such high-ranking officers who were also senior to him in age were being ordered to massage him and protested. However, Baba insisted and despite his protests, they massaged him. Internally they were annoyed with Suresh for not following their advice and staying back and for insisting on accompanying them on the Field Walk.

By then Suresh’s face had swollen considerably and he was in great pain. He was worried about how he would face his family in that condition. While returning from the Tiger’s Grave, Suresh expressed his concern to Asthana, “I will have to catch the night train to Bhagalpur. Actually I should have been there earlier today to celebrate the Chatth festival with my family. I am worried how I will explain my condition to them.” Asthana hesitantly informed Baba that Suresh had to return home that night.

“How can he go with this injury?” Baba asked. He paused for a while and said, “Let me see it. It was dark and I could not see how serious it is. Shine the torch on his face.” Asthana shone the light on Suresh’s face. Baba abruptly stretched out his finger towards Suresh’s face. Involuntarily Suresh shrank back, thinking that Baba was going to hurt his wound; but very gently, Baba touched the wound with his finger. To Suresh’s great surprise and relief, the pain in his face instantly vanished and he felt a soothing sensation. He touched his face with his hand and found that the swelling had completely disappeared. Baba gave him a gentle pat on his cheek and said, “Alright, you can go home now.” The other Margis also inspected his face and found to their utter surprise that the swelling had gone. A slight scar was the only trace of the injury. As they crossed the footbridge Baba turned around and said, “Suresh, you must run. The train is waiting for you only.”

### Occupying the Land

Later that week Kedarnath, Chandranath, Kishun, Rambahadur and some others met in Jamalpur. Baba instructed them to make plans to take immediate possession of the land and commence the construction of the jagrti without further ado. Under Kedarnath’s supervision a detailed plan was chalked out. The Margis from the Bihar Military Police were ordered to assemble at the jagrti the following Sunday before dawn. Some arrived on Saturday evening and Chandranath brought a truckload of Margi jawans (soldiers) just before sunrise on Sunday. In a lightning operation they dismantled the makeshift temple and loaded all the rubble onto the truck. Just then Bachchu and his sons, along with a few hired hoodlums, rushed over wielding big *lathis*. Kedarnath, who had positioned himself in the front with a lathi in his hand, put his training in the police force to good use and floored Bachchu with one stroke. His sons and the other hoodlums were no match for the motivated and well-trained BMP Margis and were quickly subdued. Completely unnerved by the overwhelming strength of the Margis, they fled the scene. From a distance they watched helplessly as the truck sped away loaded with the remnants of what had been their temple only a short while before to be immersed in the river Ganges in Monghyr. Minutes later, two truckloads of bricks arrived, along with several masons and manual laborers. The laborers got down to work immediately and started digging trenches for the foundation of the boundary wall. The construction of the wall began in no time using local clay as mortar to bind the bricks.

The operation was well-planned and was executed on a war footing. Bachchu’s ferocious resistance ended in a whimper. The Margis had a big piece of land in their possession and the satisfaction of easily overcoming an opponent who had appeared invincible only a few days before.

### Collective Effort

As planned, many Margis from the nearby villages and towns came to help construct the boundary wall. Realizing the vulnerability of his position over the ownership of the land, Bachchu filed an official complaint against the Margis for destroying a place of worship. He produced the initial contract signed with the landowner in an attempt to establish that he was indeed the rightful owner of the property. He also managed to prepare some semi-legal documents to reinforce his claim. Not convinced by his claim and anticipating the possibility of further tension, the local administration passed prohibitory orders to prevent Bachchu and his gang from entering the area. In the meantime the Margis quickly got on with the task of

building the wall. Baba visited the worksite to check on the progress of work twice daily, which motivated them to redouble their speed. Within a week they had completed the construction of a sturdy and huge boundary wall around the entire property.

The following Sunday, the last day of the month, a small pandal was erected in the plot, and Baba held his first darshan there. He lauded the Margis for their hard work. "I want the jagrti building to be completed with the same speed in exactly four weeks," he continued, piling on the pressure. "I will inaugurate it and hold DMC here on the 29th of December."

Initially it appeared impossible to build the jagrti in such a short time. But their success in recovering the land and Baba's appreciation of their indomitable spirit in building the boundary wall in such a short time had instilled a new vigor and confidence in everyone. They were determined to complete the task by any means in order to please their guru. In an urgently convened meeting Pranay appealed to everyone for financial contributions and their help in constructing the building within the stipulated period. Prabha, the teenage daughter of Vivekananda Singh, immediately stood up, removed her earrings, the only jewelry she possessed, and offered them to the building fund. This started the ball rolling. The exemplary action of such a young girl spurred the others to do their best. In addition to making financial contributions, several Margis took leave from their jobs to help meet Baba's deadline for the construction of the jagrti. The construction work went on round the clock, with people camping at the construction site in spite of the discomfort, the night-time chill and the mosquitoes, to work alongside the employed laborers in order to expedite the work. Those who could not take leave spent all their free hours pitching in. Advocates, college lecturers, school teachers and government officials worked alongside coolies, students, housewives and children. Margis from different towns participated in the construction by sending materials and food. Others brought musical instruments and many of the Margis danced and sang devotional songs as they worked. Indeed there was an almost carnival-like atmosphere at the construction site. Baba also paid regular visits, one of which Baban Tiwari described in an interview:

> We all worked day and night, but Baba was never out of our minds. Once it was raining very heavily, so Baba could not come to visit us. As I worked shivering in the cold, my mind became restless due to his absence. I was humming to myself, "Oh Baba, you did not come today. What's the matter? How can I stay here without you?" All I could think about was Baba and how much I was missing him. Then suddenly I saw Baba approaching. He was holding an umbrella over his head with one hand and lifting his dhoti up with the other to keep it clear of the water and mud flowing down the street due to the torrential rain. I ran up to him and asked him why he had taken so much trouble to come in this rainy weather.
>
> "You called me, so I came," was his simple reply.
>
> "Oh no, Baba," I told him. "It was just wishful thinking. I didn't actually mean that I wanted you to come physically in such rough conditions. I wasn't complaining in the hope that you would hear me and come. How could you walk all this way down these muddy, dirty streets in this terrible rain?"
>
> "How can I think of staying away when my devotee is demanding my presence?" he asked. "It is just not possible."

There were several instances of Margis falling sick due to working in the cold weather. Every evening when Baba would come to visit them, they would feel tremendously invigorated and their illness would vanish instantaneously. There were many others working in the construction site who had extraordinary experiences of Baba's blessings.

Chandranath's nephew, Ramakanta, was among those who often slept at the site and worked on the construction full-time until it was completed. One evening police officer Kuldip, who had taken a month's leave to help with the work, went on the Field Walk with Baba to the Tiger's Grave. As they walked, he took the opportunity to praise Ramakanta.

"Baba, I have never seen such a hardworking young man. He works day and night without stopping, but it is regrettable that he doesn't get the time to do much meditation."

Baba just smiled and continued walking. When Kuldip returned to the jagrti that evening, he found Ramakanta lying motionless in Baba's room in a state of divine trance. When he asked the other Margis what had happened, they told him that Ramakanta had come there to do his evening meditation at about eight o'clock and shortly afterwards had gone into samadhi. Kuldip later discovered that Ramakanta had experienced the divine state of samadhi at exactly the time that he had been talking to Baba about him during the Field Walk. His spiritual trance lasted for three hours.

The building was completed on the 27th of December 1958, exactly one day ahead of schedule. The Margis erected a large tent in front of the new jagrti and on the evening of the 29th Baba inaugurated the building and held a DMC there. While Baba was in the middle of his talk, the District Magistrate happened to come by to investigate the charges filed by Bachchu Mandal against the Margis for destroying a temple. When he saw the building, the boundary wall and hundreds of devotees listening in complete silence to Baba's lecture, he realized that he was wasting his time investigating false charges. For the sake of formality, however, he asked Vaidyanath and Akhori Himachal Prasad a few questions and subsequently returned to Monghyr with a few of Baba's books that the two Margis had gifted him. In due course he dismissed the case.

Now the Margis of Jamalpur finally had a place of their own. This was the first struggle the Margis had to confront collectively as a group and was the precursor of many others that the Marga would have to face in the coming years. On various occasions Baba reminded his disciples that struggle is an essential element of success and that struggle should be welcomed in the life of every sadhaka.

**CHAPTER 31**

# Defeat of Dogma

The inauguration of the new, spacious jagrti of Jamalpur at the end of 1958 helped to accelerate the spread of Ananda Marga. As the Marga entered its fifth year of existence, more and more people started to come to Jamalpur. With increasing numbers of people getting the opportunity to meet Baba, many were inspired to take an active role in the spread of the mission. 1959 was a highly significant year in the history of Ananda Marga. Baba added several new dimensions to the ideology and new areas of activity were developed during the course of the year. As a result the Marga began to expand in rapid strides.

### Inspiring the Downfallen

A DMC was organized in Patna on 22nd February on the occasion of the full moon. Rukundeshvar Prasad, a recently retired police officer, had just completed the construction of his new house in the city. When he heard that the Margis were organizing DMC he offered his house for Baba's stay in the hope that it would sanctify the house before his family moved in. He also proposed that the DMC be held on the roof of his house, which was big enough.

Rukundeshvar had been initiated only a few months earlier. Before his initiation he led an immoral life and had acquired many bad habits. After his initiation into spiritual practice he turned over a new leaf. However, owing to the negative impression many still had of him, some senior Margis rejected his offer outright, thinking that it was highly improper to accommodate Baba in the house of a man who had previously led an immoral life.

Baba arrived in Patna by train on 21st February. The welcoming party then took him to the Sinha Library for a short darshan. The library was also the venue for the DMC scheduled to be held the following day. A house nearby was arranged for Baba's accommodation. On reaching the library, Baba rejected the proposed venue of the DMC due to the presence of members of the public in some parts of the building. He instructed the Margis to immediately arrange an alternative place for the evening program and the DMC the following day. The Margis were very surprised by Baba's insistence on a new DMC venue and did not know what to do in such a short time. Seeing their predicament, Baba summoned Rukundeshvar and inquired, "Rukundeshvar, this place is not suitable for our program because it is a public place and a lot of people visit here. Tomorrow is Sunday, and many people will be coming to the library. So would it be possible to hold this evening's program as well as the DMC tomorrow on the roof of your house?"

Rukundeshvar could not believe his ears that Baba was himself proposing to hold the entire program in his house. Choked with emotion, he could only nod his head in affirmation.

"If it is not inconvenient, you can also arrange two rooms there for me and the attending secretary."

By then Rukundeshvar was totally overwhelmed with emotion. With tears streaming down his cheeks, he said, "Baba, I would be greatly honored if you could hold the program in my new house. There are sufficient rooms to accommodate both of you. It is newly built, and at present no one is staying there."

"Good. So now please go quickly to your house and make all the arrangements. I will finish my evening meditation and Field Walk in the meantime and will reach your place within a couple of hours. There is no need for any elaborate arrangements. I can adjust with whatever you can provide in such a short time."

Rukundeshvar prostrated before Baba and left the place forthwith. He was still dazed by the unexpected shower of grace he had received with the granting of his wish.

Baba then directed the Margis to immediately proceed to Rukundeshvar’s house in Mahendru and help him in the preparations of the evening program and DMC. They all worked together to make the place ready for the event. The district secretary, Biharilal, and some others, however, were a little disappointed with Baba’s decision. They felt that people might misunderstand Baba’s reason for staying in the house of a person who was known to have been corrupt in the past, but didn’t dare to express it to him.

The next morning Baba went to Phulwarisharif on the outskirts of Patna to meet Rambahadur, who was unwell. He asked the district secretary to accompany him. Some other Margis followed in two cars. After visiting Rambahadur they returned to Patna. On the way he stopped the vehicle for his morning walk. After walking for a while, he sat down in an open field surrounded by the Margis and narrated a story:

“Over two thousand years ago there was a very virtuous lady by the name of Madalasa. She was spiritually very evolved. However, the Puranas have distorted the history of her life. In Aryan literature, she has been portrayed as a *rakshasi* (a demon) because she belonged to the Dravidian race. Due to a false sense of superiority, the Aryans felt contempt for the Dravidians and Mongoloids (Orientals) who they depicted as demons and monsters. The Dravidians were intellectually and spiritually far more advanced than the Aryans. The Mongoloids were action-oriented and more spiritually advanced as well. The Aryans were intellectually and spiritually inferior to the other two races. Most of them performed Nature worship whereas the Dravidians and Mongoloids practiced Tantra sadhana as taught by Lord Shiva.

Coming back to Madalasa, she was to be married to Chitrasena, the King of Kashi. Before the marriage took place she informed her prospective husband, “I will marry you only on the condition that I will be solely responsible for the education and upbringing of our children. You have to give me your word that you will not interfere at all in this matter under any circumstance. If you violate your promise I will leave you.”

The King of Kashi was highly enamoured of the exceptionally beautiful Madalasa and agreed to this condition. The marriage between the two was then solemnized.

Four children were born to them. The first was named Vikranta. While Vikranta was growing in her womb, Madalasa would sit for long hours in meditation and would always remain in spiritual contemplation. Because of that, the child had inborn spiritual traits. She would put him in the cradle and sing lullabies to him in a very sweet voice, which were full of lofty spiritual truths. One of her lullabies was:

Shuddhosi buddhosi niranjanosi samsara maya parivarjitosi,
Samsara svapnam tyaja moha nidram Madalasollapamuvacha putram.

The meaning is, “O my son! You are that pure Entity; you are that all-knowing Entity; you are that spotless Entity. This world is a passing show; it is ever-changing. It is all like a dream. O my son, awaken from your sleep of ignorance and worldly infatuation and know the Ultimate Reality.”

When Vikranta was seven, Madalasa taught him meditation and gave him spiritual guidance. Vikranta grew up to be an ardent spiritual seeker and when he was about twelve Madalasa sent him to a guru for further spiritual training. Later Vikranta renounced the worldly life and become a *sannyasi*. Right from his early childhood Madalasa had inspired her son to renounce worldly life, not for his own spiritual progress but with a mission to serve society. His duty was to guide the people along the path of righteousness. Actually, Vikranta was the first person in ancient Hindu society to embrace the life of a renunciate and work as a missionary. Although the system of monks had existed much earlier, they generally led a life of leisure and worldly enjoyment and had no thought of serving society. When Vikranta renounced his

worldly life, it was a great blow to his father, the King of Kashi, as he had fondly hoped that his eldest son would succeed him on the throne.

Under Madalasa's influence and training the second son Subahu soon followed in Vikranta's footsteps.

When his third son was born, King Chitrasena decided to name him Shatrumardan, meaning 'one who would slay his enemies'. He gave him such a name thinking that it would help him develop the qualities of a warrior and thus become eligible to succeed him as the king. As she had done with her other sons, Madalasa imparted spiritual training to her third son too. He also grew up to be a spiritual seeker and renounced worldly life. The ideal of a missionary life adopted by these children at such a young age was solely due to their upbringing by Madalasa.

The king named their fourth son Alarka, which meant 'mad dog'. He thought that such a strange name would distance him from any spiritual inclination. Madalasa was not happy with the name but yielded to the king's wishes. She started to impart spiritual teachings to Alarka as well.

King Chitrasena was by now very concerned that due to Madalasa's training, all three of his sons had renounced worldly life in quest of higher spiritual knowledge. He feared that there would be no one to take over the reins of the kingdom after him. Then one day, while strolling past the palace where Madalasa lived, the king heard Madalasa singing the same spiritual lullaby to Alarka that she had sung to his other three sons.

He thought, "Madalasa has spoiled three of my sons. And now she is doing the same thing with Alarka as well. I can't let this happen."

Thinking thus, he went up to his wife and said, "Madalasa, please stop it. Your spiritual teaching has made three of our children renounce the world. Who will succeed me to the throne? I will not allow you to train Alarka in this way."

The queen replied, "Alright, I entrust you with the responsibility of bringing up Alarka. But as you have broken your word about not interfering with my way of bringing up the children, I will leave the kingdom in pursuit of my spiritual life. My presence here will not serve any further purpose."

As she was about to leave, she gave a ring to the king and said, "Please put this ring on Alarka's finger when he is a young man. Kindly convey to him my message that whenever he is in a great crisis, he should break open the ring and inside it he will find the advice that he needs." With these words Madalasa left the king's palace.

Alarka was brought up by the king who had immersed himself in material pleasures. After Madalasa's departure he degenerated and sank into a life of indulgence. Naturally, with such a defective upbringing, Alarka developed many bad habits. These became more pronounced as he grew older. When he ascended the throne of Kashi at a very young age after the death of his father, Alarka hardly had any time for his kingdom and the people. He was too engrossed in the pursuit of his own worldly pleasures. The condition of the land and the people deteriorated day by day, and the kingdom suffered greatly. The state officials ruthlessly exploited the people, as generally happens when the king does not spend time looking after the affairs of state. Unable to bear all this, the people longed for a change of administration but did not know how to bring it about.

Vikranta, who was then living in a hermitage as a renunciant, heard about the miseries of the people of Kashi. He approached the king of neighboring Koshala and said, "I am the eldest brother of King Alarka. The kingdom actually belongs to me. You also know about the sorry state of affairs in Kashi. I therefore request you to please march with your army to Kashi, conquer it and hand it over to me."

The King of Koshala was a righteous person. He thought the proposal to be a wise one and invaded Kashi. As no one was ready to support the unpopular Alarka, Kashi was conquered without a fight. Alarka then fled the kingdom to save himself.

Vikranta then beseeched the King of Koshala, "I requested you to attack Kashi only to teach Alarka a lesson. My duty is now over. Please hand the kingdom back to Alarka and ask him to rule it properly and take care of the needs of the people. I hope that Alarka will now rule justly." Vikranta then returned to his hermitage.

Alarka, however, had fled Kashi during the invasion by the Koshala army. To avoid being captured, he hid in various places until he reached a forest. There, helpless and unaccustomed to a life of hardship, he realized that he was in deep trouble. As he pondered over his fate, his eyes suddenly fell upon the ring given to him by his mother, and he remembered her counsel. He was indeed in a grave crisis and badly needed guidance. So, he broke open the ring and found some advice written on a small piece of cloth. The first was, "Do not have any desire, but if that is not possible, then have only the desire for *moksha* (salvation)." The second was, "Do not keep any type of company, but if that is not possible, keep *satsanga* (good company)."

Alarka thought, "It is not possible for me to be desireless. And I have committed such evil deeds, so how can I get moksha? Regarding the second advice, it is not possible for me to live without company, but let me keep good company. This is what I can do."

Young Alarka gave up all ambitions of regaining the kingdom and went out in search of ideal company. His quest brought him to the jungles of what is today western Birbhum of West Bengal where the great sage Ashtavakra was doing penance. This sacred spot was later named Vakreshvar after the sage Ashtavakra. Alarka asked the sage a number of questions. These questions and Ashtavakra's answers came to be known as the *Ashtavakra Samhita* and appears in the *Markandeya Purana* as narrated by Dattatreya. Alarka was the first person to be initiated into *Rajadhiraja Yoga*, the process of controlling all the chakras and their associated propensities. Due to his sadhana and the good company he kept, Alarka eventually became an elevated soul.

Meanwhile, the King of Koshala could not find Alarka. He also had no desire whatsoever to extend the borders of his own kingdom to include Kashi. He therefore decided to temporarily rule Kashi as its regent, and if either Vikranta or Alarka turned up, he would hand over the reins of the kingdom to him.

The King of Koshala ruled Kashi justly. After the passage of a few years, Vikranta thought one day, "I asked the King of Koshala to invade Kashi only to reform Alarka. I guess now he must be ruling Kashi in a proper way. Why don't I go and see him?" With this thought he set out for Kashi.

At the same time, a thought arose in Alarka's mind, who was by now reformed: "Vikranta must be ruling excellently. He was the one who opened my eyes. I should go and express my gratitude to him for helping me to change the defective course of my life." Thus, Alarka also left his hermitage and set out for Kashi.

On their way to Kashi the two brothers chanced to meet each other. They embraced with great affection and exchanged news about what had happened since Alarka fled Kashi. Vikranta was overjoyed at the great transformation in his brother. They then proceeded towards the court of the King of Koshala. When they arrived, the king hurried to meet them. He said, "You two have really burdened me with the administration of Kashi when I already had enough to keep me busy in my own kingdom of Koshala. Now that you have come, please take back your kingdom and release me from the burden of administering Kashi."

However, neither Vikranta nor Alarka was ready to do this. While Vikranta from the beginning had no attraction for material pursuits, Alarka had eventually acquired a keen attraction for the divine world. Both of them expressed their unwillingness to rule Kashi, and requested the King of Koshala to continue to govern it as part of his kingdom. Left with no choice, the king acceded to their request.

Before concluding this narration, Baba commented that the history of Madalasa, Alarka, and Ashtavakra had been distorted in several stories of the Puranas. He then ended by asking a question. "There are four people here — Madalasa, Vikranta, Alarka, and the King of Koshala. Now tell me which character in this story would inspire the common man the most and give me the reason why."

The Margis expressed their personal views. Everyone had a different opinion. Some selected Madalasa because although she belonged to a royal household, she had inspired all her children to become sadhakas. Others chose Vikranta because although he was a sannyasi, he did not forget society. When it was necessary, he came back to fulfil his responsibilities to society. Yet others favored the King of Koshala as he was a dharmic ruler and a righteous person.

After listening to all their views Baba said, "All of them were great human beings. However, the most inspiring character is the one who is not only great himself but whose life can also motivate others. Common people cannot identify themselves with Madalasa, Vikranta, or the King of Koshala, but Alarka has that characteristic. A great majority of people, in fact, almost everyone, commits mistakes.
